The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen has reported that it intercepted a drone launched by the Houthis towards Saudi Arabia’s Mecca region.
The drone was “intercepted and destroyed” on Friday morning, coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said in a social media post. It was also reported that a missile aimed at western Saudi Arabia was earlier brought down, as hostilities between the Riyadh-backed Yemen government and Iran-backed Houthis continue to escalate.
A Houthi spokesperson denied targeting the Muslim holy city or surrounding region, reiterating that the group’s cross-border attacks remain strictly focused on Saudi energy and military infrastructure.
The Saudi-led coalition has previously accused the Houthis of launching drones towards Islam’s two holiest cities: Mecca and Medina.
“Our operations target [Saudi] oil facilities and military bases, and there is no longer anyone in this world who believes these fabrications and lies propagated by the criminal Al Saud regime,” the Houthi spokesman wrote.
Escalating hostilities
The opposing claims come as hostilities continue with no sign of slowing, and humanitarian agencies warn of worsening conditions for civilians.
On Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards the kingdom’s eastern region. It later said two ballistic missiles launched towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh, were also intercepted and destroyed.
Al-Malki reported early on Friday that the coalition’s air defences intercepted and destroyed a Houthi cruise missile that targeted western Saudi Arabia.
Media outlets affiliated with the Houthis reported later that coalition air attacks were targeting the Mahliyah district in Marib, Haifan in Taiz, and Huwaishan in al-Jawf in the country.
Al Jazeera Arabic’s Hadeel al-Yamani reported from Taiz that fighting along the front lines was persisting.
The governor of Taiz said the city was suffering heavy shelling, with residential neighbourhoods taking hits.
“Aircraft can be heard frequently over the city, which remains under a suffocating siege, with no medical supplies, water or fuel getting in,” al-Yamani reported.
“On the western front, there were intermittent clashes around dawn. The northern fronts were relatively calm, but still saw sporadic fighting. There has been a notable escalation in hostilities around Jabal Saber and Jabal Habashi,” he said.

articles.title: Hormuz shipping crisis deepens as Iran reports tanker fires, Houthis target Saudi oil facilities - The News Pakistan
articles.summary: Hormuz shipping crisis deepens as Iran reports tanker fires, Houthis target Saudi oil facilities  The News Pakistan
articles.full_text:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said four oil tankers had caught fire and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz, while separate maritime security reports pointed to further attacks on commercial shipping, as the widening conflict involving Iran, the United States and Israel continued to threaten critical energy infrastructure across the Gulf.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said the tankers had attempted to navigate routes it described as unauthorised. In its latest statement, it reported that a fourth vessel, carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil, had struck a naval mine, suffered a powerful explosion and caught fire, Iranian state media reported on Friday.
An earlier IRGC Navy statement had reported that another tanker carrying two million barrels of crude had struck a mine.
Reuters could not independently verify the Iranian military's account.
Separately, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said it had received a report that a crude oil tanker was struck by an unknown projectile while completing an outbound transit through the strait.
In an earlier incident report, UKMTO said a vessel had been hit on its port side about 40 nautical miles (74km) south of Iran's Lavan Island, triggering a fire on board. Its crew were reported safe, with no environmental impact.
It was not immediately clear whether the vessels involved in the UKMTO reports were among the four tankers cited by Iran.
In a separate report on Friday, Reuters said UKMTO had reported a tanker being struck by explosive devices attached to a small boat, in what maritime sources described as the first known successful limpet-mine attack in the waterway since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in February.
The incidents underline the growing dangers to commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic passage connecting the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea through which around a fifth of the world's oil supplies passed before the conflict.
Iranian state media also reported that its forces had downed and captured an MQM-170 US drone over Qeshm Island, near the Strait of Hormuz. There was no immediate US military response to that claim, which Reuters could not independently verify.
Tehran also said it had destroyed an unmanned US vessel in the eastern Strait of Hormuz.
However, the US military's Central Command rejected the claim, saying all American unmanned surface vessels in the Middle East were accounted for, including a squadron of advanced sea drones patrolling the waterway.
The latest maritime incidents come amid heightened tensions following US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February and subsequent Iranian attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure across the region.
Reuters reported earlier this month that Iran had shifted towards intensifying attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, seeking to keep oil prices elevated and increase pressure on Washington.
At least seven incidents involving tankers were reported during a week in early October, according to maritime intelligence service Marisks. The incidents included attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, raising concerns over the security of energy exports from the Gulf.
The maritime security crisis has coincided with a renewed Houthi campaign against Saudi Arabia, further widening the conflict's geographical reach.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group said on Thursday it had attacked several Saudi energy facilities, including the Ras Tanura refinery, the Rabigh refinery and a production facility at Abqaiq owned by state oil giant Saudi Aramco.
A Saudi-led coalition also said it had intercepted a cruise missile launched by the Houthis towards the kingdom's western region.
The attacks followed repeated Houthi strikes on Saudi airports, oil installations and other critical infrastructure this month, including an October 10 attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, according to Reuters.
The Houthis have also threatened further attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities, warning civilians, workers and international shipping companies to stay away from sites they consider legitimate targets.
The renewed offensive has severely disrupted Saudi aviation. According to aviation analytics firm Cirium, 4,071 of 4,736 scheduled flights at Riyadh's airport, or 86%, were cancelled between October 8 and October 25.
More than 7,800 flights, accounting for 45% of scheduled departures across Saudi airports, were cancelled during the same period.
The United States on Friday confirmed that it had ordered non-emergency government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia, effective October 23, citing security risks from Houthi attacks on civilian airports and critical infrastructure.
The US embassy in Riyadh warned American citizens of possible further attacks, airspace closures, flight cancellations and other travel disruptions.
The fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government has intensified in recent weeks, opening another volatile front in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran.
A truce between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition collapsed in July. The group subsequently declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia, attacked Saudi vessels and the East-West pipeline, and seized Yemen's Red Sea coastline and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, according to Reuters.
The military escalation has continued despite diplomatic efforts involving regional powers to prevent the conflict from spreading further.
Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on Friday as part of coordinated efforts to reach an agreement between Washington and Tehran, an official briefed on the discussions told Reuters.
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that Vice President JD Vance had reached out to Iran to help the country obtain medical supplies, following reports that Vance had written to Tehran's top security official in an effort to revive peace negotiations.
Iran has confirmed receiving Vance's letter but has yet to respond, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency. Tehran has said Washington must meet its conditions for an agreement.
Earlier this week, Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials met Iranian leaders in Tehran and agreed to continue discussions, although the agenda and substance of the talks have not been disclosed.
Pakistan's military said on Friday it was "cautiously optimistic" about Islamabad's mediation efforts, following two visits to Tehran this month by Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin accompanied Munir during his latest visit.
The diplomatic engagement comes against the backdrop of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on August 7, under which an attack on any signatory is to be treated as an attack on all.
Pakistan's military spokesman Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said the agreement did not rule out additional members, including Iran, although any expansion would require a decision by the signatories' political leadership.
The mounting security risks have added to concerns over global energy supplies, with the Strait of Hormuz remaining a critical chokepoint for crude oil and fuel shipments.
Oil prices rose more than 2% on Friday, settling at their highest levels since late April as traders weighed the possibility of further escalation and the risks to supplies from the Middle East.
Brent crude futures for December delivery settled $2.76 higher, or 2.4%, at $117.64 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate rose $2.12, or 2.08%, to $104.12.
For October, Brent gained 13.6%, while WTI rose 15.2%.
The attacks have raised concerns about the ability of Gulf producers to maintain exports through both the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes, particularly as Saudi Arabia faces renewed threats to its oil infrastructure and Red Sea shipping access.
Saudi crude exports nevertheless increased in October compared with September, according to two of three ship-tracking companies cited by Reuters, despite Iranian attacks on shipping and Houthi claims of strikes on Saudi energy facilities.
With Washington and Tehran yet to reach an agreement, the combination of maritime attacks, renewed fighting in Yemen and threats to Gulf energy infrastructure continues to complicate diplomatic efforts to contain the eight-month-old conflict.

articles.title: Qatar’s LNG Empire Is Being Strangled by the War with Iran - Todayville
articles.summary: Qatar’s LNG Empire Is Being Strangled by the War with Iran  Todayville
articles.full_text:
The wealth of the Gulf states depends upon their ability to export energy to the rest of the world. Qatar is a particularly dangerous case because its economy depends heavily upon liquefied natural gas (LNG), and nearly all of that export trade must pass through the Strait of Hormuz. Qatar’s LNG exports had collapsed by 96% by the end of August. The country lost an estimated $24 billion in gas sales during the first six months of the conflict, equivalent to approximately five months of its 2025 gas income. This is an extraordinary loss for a nation that has built its wealth upon supplying energy to the global economy.
The situation has become so desperate that QatarEnergy, once one of the world’s dominant LNG exporters, is now purchasing American natural gas to fulfill its international obligations. QatarEnergy has reportedly entered into a 30-year agreement with Cheniere Energy to purchase 4 million metric tons of LNG annually through 2054, with deliveries expected to begin in the 2030s. The company is also negotiating with Venture Global for another 3 million tons annually. Qatar possesses one of the largest natural gas reserves on the planet, yet it is arranging to buy LNG from its American competitors because it cannot reliably deliver its own product to customers. The country has not run out of gas. It has lost reliable access to the shipping routes necessary to sell it.
Iranian attacks have compounded the disaster. Two production trains at Qatar’s Ras Laffan complex were damaged, removing approximately 17% of the country’s LNG export capacity. Repairs could take three years. The remaining production capacity is of limited economic value if the tankers cannot safely reach international markets. QatarEnergy has repeatedly declared force majeure on supply contracts, leaving customers in Asia and Europe scrambling for replacement shipments. Qatar had exported only 18 LNG cargoes through the end of August, compared with 509 during the same period in 2025. Those numbers demonstrate how thoroughly the conflict disrupted one of the world’s most important energy suppliers.
The geographical problem is especially severe. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates possess oil pipelines that can move some crude production toward ports outside the Strait of Hormuz. Qatar does not enjoy that flexibility. Natural gas cannot simply be loaded onto an ordinary tanker or pumped through an existing crude oil pipeline. LNG requires specialized liquefaction facilities, storage infrastructure, and vessels capable of maintaining extremely low temperatures. Constructing an alternative export system across Saudi Arabia or the UAE would require enormous investment, new infrastructure, and political agreements, none of which would provide immediate relief. Qatar is effectively trapped by its geography. Its principal source of national income depends upon a maritime passage that Iran can threaten at any moment.
This is precisely why I have emphasized the sovereign debt problems developing throughout the Middle East. Governments have built spending commitments around the assumption that energy revenues will continue flowing. Qatar has accumulated substantial financial reserves and overseas investments, which provide it with more protection than many other countries. Nevertheless, reserves are not an unlimited substitute for income. The government still has to finance public services, infrastructure, salaries, subsidies, and existing obligations while its principal export industry struggles to operate. The longer the disruption continues, the more pressure there will be to postpone spending, reconsider investment commitments, and conserve available liquidity.
Qatar recorded a budget deficit of approximately $5.8 billion in the second quarter of 2026, its largest quarterly shortfall in nearly a decade. LNG exports fell from roughly 20 million tons per quarter before the war to less than 2 million tons between April and June. Government revenues dropped approximately 30%, while expenditures declined only 2.6%.
Nonessential construction, discretionary spending, and projects that don’t contribute directly to economic survival become harder to justify. Qatar has spent decades transforming its energy wealth into enormous infrastructure projects, international investments, and an expanding global presence. That model works exceptionally well when LNG revenues arrive without interruption. When the primary source of income is suddenly restricted, the government must reassess how long it can sustain its commitments. There is no indication that every nonessential project has been canceled, but the financial incentive to delay discretionary expenditures is unmistakable.
The consequences are also being felt throughout Asia and Europe. India, Bangladesh, and other major LNG importers have been forced to seek alternative supplies, while European gas storage remains vulnerable ahead of winter. Qatar previously supplied approximately one-fifth of global LNG trade. Removing that volume from international markets does not simply hurt Qatar. It creates competition for the remaining available gas, increases transportation and insurance costs, and places additional pressure on countries that depend upon imported energy. Europe has already undermined its industrial competitiveness through expensive energy policies and its confrontation with Russia. Another prolonged disruption to natural gas supplies will only make matters worse.
Qatar is far from bankrupt, and it possesses substantial financial assets that can help it endure this crisis. But there is a tremendous difference between possessing wealth and generating the income required to sustain an economy. A nation cannot indefinitely finance its obligations by drawing down reserves while its primary export industry remains constrained. Qatar has begun restoring some LNG shipments through Hormuz, but those voyages remain vulnerable to renewed attacks. Even a partial recovery does not eliminate the problem when the entire economic structure depends upon safe passage through one narrow waterway.
I have maintained that the Middle East War Cycle would have consequences far beyond the battlefield. Qatar demonstrates how a country can become an economic casualty of a war even when it is not the principal combatant. The government has little choice but to conserve its financial resources, protect its remaining energy infrastructure, and hope that shipping conditions improve before the damage becomes permanent. Its enormous gas reserves have not disappeared, but those reserves cannot pay the bills if they cannot reach the customer. The longer this conflict continues, the more governments throughout the region will discover that their financial security was built upon assumptions about peace and uninterrupted trade that no longer hold.

QatarEnergy Secures US LNG to Hedge Against Strait of Hormuz Disruptions
QatarEnergy’s LNG Strategy Amid Geopolitical Risks
By Andrew Mills and Maha El Dahan
DOHA, Oct 29 (Reuters) - QatarEnergy is buying long-term supplies of liquefied natural gas from the US and other producers as part of a trading strategy designed to generate revenue if exports through the Strait of Hormuz are disrupted in the future, CEO Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi told Reuters on Thursday.
"In a scenario where you have a closure of the strait, which is the true contingency that we're looking to have, you'd immediately see a spike in gas price and you'll be able to generate revenue for QatarEnergy that otherwise wouldn't be generated," Kaabi, who is also the minister of state for energy affairs, said of the plan.
Kaabi's remarks reveal for the first time how Qatar, one of the world's largest LNG producers, plans to offset lost income from the Iran war and protect revenue against future disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
Major LNG Supply Agreements
The company signed a 20-year agreement on Thursday to buy 3 million metric tons per year (mtpa) from Woodside's US facilities. Last week it signed two agreements with Cheniere Energy for up to 4 mtpa through 2054 from its Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi plants. Together, the deals amount to 7 mtpa in the past two weeks.
"There's more to come," Kaabi said. Cheniere deliveries are not expected to begin until 2031.
Trading Edge and Strategic Rationale
TRADING EDGE
Kaabi, appointed CEO of the state energy giant in 2014, said the strategy was his idea and took shape about three months ago after QatarEnergy studied and ruled out pipeline options.
"As we have seen, pipelines and pump stations or compression stations can be also targets."
The strategy builds on QatarEnergy's LNG expertise, trading operation and shipping fleet. It requires no capital spending and is far cheaper than building pipelines or extra LNG trains, he said.
"In normal circumstances you'd make a reasonable return and in critical circumstances — however that comes out and how long it is — you have actual proof today of what you could make."
Impact of Recent Disruptions
QatarEnergy halted LNG production in early March after several days of Iranian missile attacks on Qatar. It declared force majeure to affected buyers on March 4.
Qatar accounts for around a fifth of global LNG exports, all of which pass through Hormuz. The company has extended force majeure until the end of 2026.
Kaabi said being unable to ship volumes had taken a heavy toll on revenue.
Leveraging QatarEnergy’s Assets
QatarEnergy believes it can leverage its fleet of about 200 LNG tankers, the world's largest, as well as QatarEnergy Trading, which Kaabi said will soon become the world's largest gas trading platform.
"When you have the arbitrage capability that we have, the volume, number of ships, all the capabilities that we have, that's why you can do it," Kaabi said.
The hedge targets a market transformed after Iran responded to a war launched by the US and Israel on February 28 by effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz, a vital chokepoint through which a fifth of the world's oil and LNG shipments pass.
QatarEnergy can profit from the gap between lower US gas prices and higher European prices, Kaabi said.
"You can imagine the arbitrage you can make, and that would make up some of the loss."
Future Prospects and Expansion Plans
MORE DEALS TO COME
Kaabi said he expects QatarEnergy to sign more 20- to 25-year supply agreements with US and other producers this year.
The company's target is "much higher" than 7 mtpa, though Kaabi declined to give a figure. He said QatarEnergy was in talks with "everybody", including Venture Global, and would buy from whichever supplier offered the best commercial terms. Reuters reported last week that Venture Global is in advanced talks to supply 3 mtpa.
Kaabi said QatarEnergy cannot offer US volumes to long-term customers as a backup to Hormuz disruptions because long-term customer contracts are point-to-point — requiring deliveries from specific export terminals to specific destinations. He added that customers had been understanding of the disruption.
Damage and Recovery Efforts
Iranian missile strikes on QatarEnergy's main Ras Laffan gas processing facility in March damaged two of its 14 LNG trains, affecting combined capacity of 12.8 mtpa and knocking out about 17% of Qatar's export capacity. QatarEnergy said in March the damage would cost about $20 billion a year in lost revenue.
Kaabi said on Thursday that repairs to the two trains would take about three years. The Pearl gas-to-liquids plant, a joint venture between QatarEnergy and Shell that was also damaged in the attack, should return to service by the first quarter of 2027, he said.
He said Qatar could restart full LNG production within a week of a peace deal, provided ships were available. Output would be limited to about 83% of pre-war levels until the damaged trains return.
Long-Term Expansion and Diplomatic Efforts
Kaabi said no announced project had been cancelled. Ras Laffan has capacity of 77 mtpa, and Qatar's plan to expand LNG output to 142 mtpa remains unchanged, with all contracts awarded, he said. North Field East, South and West are all proceeding. The first North Field train is expected to start up in the first quarter of next year, although production would require a US-Iran peace deal to be in place.
Kaabi said he had met Iran's acting petroleum minister twice in recent weeks to explore oil and gas cooperation once the war ends.
(Reporting by Andrew Mills in Doha and Maha El Dahan in Dubai. Editing by Mark Potter)

articles.title: US and Israel target 77 sites in Iran as tanker blasts rock Strait of Hormuz - bankingnews.gr

The Middle East faces the prospect of a third, even more destructive military confrontation between the US, Israel, and Iran.
The threat is no longer limited to military facilities or nuclear infrastructure.
At the center of circulating scenarios lies the economic and social functioning of the Islamic Republic itself: power generation stations, bridges, energy grids, refineries, and vital installations.
The critical question is whether Donald Trump will again choose the path of military escalation, following the recommendations of Benjamin Netanyahu and the most aggressive circles of the American government, or whether he will permit diplomacy to avert a conflict with incalculable consequences.
The history of prior confrontations has fostered a deep conviction in Tehran: military campaigns against Iran do not constitute isolated episodes, but successive phases of a broader strategy of coercion.
From the twelve-day war to the clash that began with the assassination of Ali Khamenei on February 28, 2026, the Iranian leadership sees an ongoing effort to weaken the country and impose political terms through military power.
The infrastructure war and the threat of national destruction: The 77 US, Israel targets
Particularly alarming scenarios regarding a potential American-Israeli operation are circulating across Arab media.
Massive strikes against the power grid, transport arteries, and industrial facilities of Iran are cited.
Certain unconfirmed reports point to attacks on 68 power distribution facilities, nine power generation stations, and dozens of bridges across 31 Iranian provinces.
Analysts speak of 77 targets in total.
Other scenarios include nuclear facilities in Natanz and Fordow, military infrastructure in Parchin, and even the refinery in Abadan.
An extensive strike against vital civilian infrastructure would not constitute merely a military operation.
It could trigger a humanitarian catastrophe, depriving millions of citizens of electricity, water, fuel, and essential services.
This represents the most perilous form of coercive warfare: attempting to enforce political capitulation through the paralysis of an entire society.
Chris Murphy reveals the danger
Anxiety is not confined to Tehran.
Inside the US itself, Democratic Senator Chris Murphy issued a particularly serious warning.
He characterized the plan as «insane», warning that it will not achieve its goals and will provoke a fresh cycle of devastating escalation.
He also voiced concerns regarding the consequences for the rule of law.
His intervention carries distinct significance because it undermines the argument that a new attack can serve as a brief, controlled military operation.
Iran is not a country without retaliatory capabilities.
It possesses significant military power, missile capabilities, and the geographic position to decisively influence the security of the Persian Gulf.
Therefore, anyone designing a new confrontation under the expectation that Tehran will passively accept the destruction of its infrastructure risks committing a dangerous strategic error.
Chris Murphy
Hormuz ablaze: Explosion on supertanker carrying 2,000,000 barrels of oil, third strike in a single day
At the same time, a dangerous new escalation unfolds in the Strait of Hormuz, as the Revolutionary Guards of Iran announced that a supertanker transporting more than two million barrels of oil struck a naval mine, triggering a powerful explosion and fire.
According to the Iranian agency Tasnim, the statement from the Navy of the Revolutionary Guards was issued on Friday, October 30, noting that the vessel was attempting to transit an unauthorized maritime route.
The supertanker remains ablaze at the entrance of the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz.
According to Tehran, this represents the third tanker struck within the same day, intensifying concerns over the safety of international navigation.
Iranian authorities maintain that the previous two vessels ignored warnings and attempted to navigate through restricted areas despite the hazards.
The new weapon of Iran in the Strait of Hormuz: Limpet mines change the rules of war
Concurrently, the military confrontation in the Persian Gulf acquires a new dimension, as developments in the Strait of Hormuz expose the vulnerability of international shipping to low-cost means.
According to a report by Reuters, the Panama-flagged tanker Louise 1 was struck by two magnetic limpet mines attached to its hull by a small boat.
The detonations caused a fire in the engine room and the temporary immobilization of the ship.
The crew remained safe and the tanker later resumed its course.
The identity of the perpetrators has not been confirmed.
The development holds notable strategic interest, as Reuters had previously revealed on October 14, citing two senior Iranian officials, that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) is altering its tactics against vessels it deems in violation of transit restrictions.
The significance of this tactical shift is immense.
Iran does not need to pursue a conventional naval battle with the US to provoke severe disruption in energy transport.
Even limited incidents can elevate insurance premiums, deter shipping companies, and weigh heavily on the global oil market.
The letter of JD Vance and the new diplomatic channel
Amid this hazardous environment, one initiative carries particular weight: the direct communication of American Vice President JD Vance with Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council of Iran and former commander of the Revolutionary Guards.
According to The Washington Post on October 29, the White House now considers Rezaei one of the key figures capable of securing internal consensus for a deal.
Vance reportedly expressed willingness even for an in-person meeting, focused on a new negotiating process grounded in the national interests of both sides.
The development serves as an indirect admission that American policy cannot be confined to displays of military might.
Washington seeks commitments regarding the Iranian nuclear program.
Tehran, correspondingly, demands respect for its sovereignty, lifting of sanctions, unfreezing of blocked assets, and an end to hostilities.
The issue, consequently, is not merely who sits at the negotiating table, but whether the US is willing to abandon the posture whereby Iran must capitulate first and receive concessions only afterward.
Why Washington turns to Mohsen Rezaei
The choice of Rezaei is not accidental.
Unlike a traditional diplomat, he brings decades of experience within the military and political apparatus of the Islamic Republic.
American assessments, as presented in The Washington Post, view him as a figure with direct access to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei and influence over the machinery shaping strategic decisions.
This gains prominence following earlier contacts between Vance and Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf in Islamabad, which failed to yield a lasting settlement.
However, reaching out to Rezaei does not necessarily imply sidelining Ghalibaf or Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
On the contrary, it may signal that the American side now recognizes that no agreement can be enforced by bypassing the core national security architecture of Iran.
This represents the very contradiction of American strategy: those portrayed for years as unyielding adversaries of the West are acknowledged today as potential guarantors of a viable peace.
Tehran does not accept diplomacy under threat
The greatest obstacle in talks remains the deficit of trust.
The Iranian leadership has repeatedly experienced diplomatic processes that failed to prevent military escalation.
For this reason, it treats every fresh American initiative with skepticism whenever it is accompanied by threats of bombardment.
According to The Guardian, Ghalibaf insists that progress is possible only if seven Iranian conditions are accepted, which include lifting sanctions and ending war across various fronts, including Lebanon.
The disagreement focuses primarily on the sequencing of commitments.
The US demands specific Iranian nuclear concessions first.
Iran refuses to relinquish its primary negotiating assets without prior, verifiable American actions.
This is not an insignificant procedural dispute. It touches the core of national sovereignty and the credibility of any future accord.
A settlement perceived by Iranian society as the byproduct of military extortion will struggle to gain durable political footing.
Mediators and the fear of a regional explosion
Qatar has assumed a particularly significant role in recent diplomatic contacts, while Pakistan, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia take part in efforts to prevent a renewed clash.
On October 30, a new mission of Qatari mediators to Tehran was reported, coordinated with Washington.
Up to that moment, no official Iranian response to the letter from Vance had been confirmed.
Regional governments understand that a third war will not necessarily remain contained within Iranian borders.
The Strait of Hormuz represents a vital artery for international energy trade.
A full-scale confrontation could trigger energy shocks, threaten commercial shipping, and generate unprecedented risks for Gulf economies.
Most critically, military escalation could unleash dynamics that neither Washington nor Israel would be able to fully control.
The strategic dilemma of Trump
The Trump administration faces a choice transcending partisan political conflict with Iran.
It can pursue another round of military strikes, hoping that economic exhaustion will force Tehran to back down.
Or it can recognize that previous operations failed to secure a durable political settlement.
The second path does not require adopting all Iranian positions.
It requires recognizing Iran as a state with legitimate security interests and the right to negotiate without the threat of national annihilation.

Qatar is awaiting a response from Tehran to a new proposal that could see Iran take a limited step on its nuclear program in exchange for sanctions relief and potentially the release of frozen funds, two regional diplomats told The Jerusalem Post. The response could come as early as Thursday.
The measure under consideration would involve allowing inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to return to Iran’s nuclear sites in return for sanctions relief.
On Tuesday, IAEA Director-General Rafael Grossi briefed members of the UN Security Council, saying that only the return of inspectors to the ground could provide an accurate picture of the current state of Iran’s nuclear program.
"I invite Iran to work with the IAEA without any further delay to clarify outstanding safeguards questions and to give the IAEA the information and access the agency requires, so that it can verify all relevant facilities and material, as is Iran's legal obligation," Grossi said.
The proposal comes amid continued difficulties in negotiations between Washington and Tehran. Iran has demanded that the US lift its blockade and provide some sanctions relief before discussions on its nuclear program can begin. The Trump administration, however, has insisted that Iran take an initial step on the nuclear issue from the outset of any agreement.
Potentially last opportunity for Iran to make a deal before Trump decides to strike
The return of IAEA inspectors could offer a potential starting point for bridging the gap between the two sides, while allowing the international community to assess the status of Iran’s nuclear activities.
Senior officials from the mediating countries told Iranian officials that this deal might be "the last chance before President Trump might decide to launch a military operation against Iran".
“As President Trump stated, Iran is in very bad condition, both economically and militarily, and the blockade will remain in full force and effect, with oil flowing in record numbers of barrels through the Hormuz Strait.
"The United States will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections", Anna Kelly, White House Principal Deputy Press Secretary, told the Jerusalem Post. The midterms will be held next Tuesday. articles.title: Abraham Accords still offer hope for Saudi-Israeli peace - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: Abraham Accords still offer hope for Saudi-Israeli peace  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
The recent developments surrounding the Mecca Pact raise important questions about the future of Saudi Arabia’s relationship with Israel and the broader prospects for expanding the Abraham Accords.
While criticism of Israel’s regional policies may reflect political concerns, it is equally important to examine the wider security environment, Israel’s legitimate national security interests, and the strategic consequences of allowing regional disagreements to overshadow opportunities for peace.
The path toward a more stable Middle East should not be defined by diplomatic isolation or permanent confrontation with Israel. Instead, it should be shaped by constructive engagement, mutual recognition, security cooperation, and a commitment to resolving disputes through diplomacy.
The Mecca Pact may complicate the political environment for normalization, but it does not necessarily close the door to a future Saudi-Israeli partnership.
Saudi Arabia may have reasons to strengthen its defense relationships with Pakistan and Turkey. However, such partnerships need not be directed against Israel or interpreted as a rejection of the Abraham Accords. Regional security arrangements are most constructive when they reduce the risk of conflict rather than reinforce divisions between competing political blocs.
Israel faces a complex security environment involving threats from Iran and its regional partners, alongside continuing concerns over terrorism, missile attacks, and the security of its population. These concerns deserve serious consideration in any balanced assessment of Middle Eastern stability. Criticism of Israeli government policies should not obscure Israel’s right to protect its citizens or the importance of preventing attacks on civilians.
For Riyadh, the strategic opportunity lies in maintaining its independent diplomatic relationships while exploring whether engagement with Israel could contribute to a more secure and economically integrated region. Saudi Arabia can retain strong ties with Pakistan and Turkey without making its future relationship with Israel a zero-sum choice.
The Abraham Accords have demonstrated that Arab-Israeli relations need not remain permanently defined by historical hostility. The United Arab Emirates and Bahrain established diplomatic relations with Israel in 2020, creating new opportunities for commercial exchange, technological collaboration, and people-to-people engagement.
The economic relationship between the UAE and Israel provides a practical illustration of this potential. According to figures reported by the UAE Foreign Ministry, bilateral merchandise trade reached approximately $3.2 billion in 2025. This demonstrates the tangible possibilities of cooperation, although the benefits for Saudi Arabia would depend on the terms and scope of any future agreement.
Normalization with Israel provides opportunities for Saudi Arabia
For Saudi Arabia, normalization could open opportunities in advanced technology, artificial intelligence, agriculture, water security, healthcare, renewable energy, logistics, and regional investment. For Israel, stronger relations with the kingdom could broaden its regional economic partnerships and create additional channels for diplomatic engagement.
These possibilities should not be dismissed because of political disagreements. A sustainable agreement could be based on diplomatic recognition of Israel, civilian protection, and regional security.
On November 18, 2025, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman publicly expressed Saudi Arabia’s interest in joining the Abraham Accords. His remarks remain an important reference point for assessing Riyadh’s long-term position.
Saudi Arabia’s long-term economic transformation, its international partnerships, and its interest in regional stability provide reasons to keep diplomatic channels with Israel open. The precise conditions for normalization remain a matter for the parties concerned, but the prospect itself should not be abandoned prematurely.
A lasting agreement would require difficult negotiations, political leadership, and reciprocal commitments. Israel would need to see credible assurances regarding its security, while Saudi Arabia would need a diplomatic framework that addresses its regional priorities. International partners, particularly the United States, could play an important role in bridging these concerns.
The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute reported that Middle Eastern military expenditure reached approximately $218 billion in 2025. Israel’s estimated military spending was around $48.3 billion, reflecting the substantial security pressures facing the country.
These figures illustrate the scale of regional investment in defense, although they do not establish that any single state is responsible for the region’s instability. They also reinforce the importance of credible deterrence, crisis-management mechanisms, and sustained diplomatic engagement.
Regional security cannot be achieved by treating Israel’s concerns as secondary or by assuming that diplomatic pressure alone will resolve security disputes. Israeli civilians, like civilians elsewhere in the region, have a fundamental interest in living without the threat of terrorism, indiscriminate attacks, or persistent insecurity.
Protecting civilians and respecting international humanitarian law must remain essential principles for every party. A credible peace strategy should address Israeli security concerns.
The Mecca Pact should consequently be assessed by how it contributes to stability in practice. If it strengthens deterrence while preserving diplomatic flexibility, it could have a constructive role. If it encourages a more polarized regional order in which Israel is treated as a permanent adversary, the prospects for normalization and cooperation could deteriorate.
Regional and international stakeholders, including the United States, should support Saudi Arabia’s constructive engagement with Israel and consider the Abraham Accords a valuable framework for advancing regional dialogue, economic cooperation, and peaceful coexistence.
This position is grounded in the strategic view that lasting peace is more likely to emerge through sustained engagement than through indefinite isolation.
Supporting Israel’s security does not require endorsing every policy of its government. Responsible diplomacy must make room for both principles.
For Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey, there is an opportunity to contribute to a regional environment in which security partnerships and diplomatic engagement reinforce one another. Their relationships with the United States and other international actors could help facilitate dialogue, reduce tensions and support a negotiated political future.
Two priorities should guide future diplomacy:
• Protect Israel’s legitimate security interests: Ensure that any regional peace framework addresses threats to Israeli civilians and establishes credible mechanisms to prevent renewed violence.
• Keep Saudi-Israeli normalization viable: Encourage practical diplomatic initiatives and reciprocal commitments rather than allowing political disagreements to become permanent barriers to engagement.
The Mecca Pact may not necessarily complicate Saudi Arabia’s path toward normalization, although it may if criticism of Israel becomes more prominent in regional political discourse. Nevertheless, it should not automatically be interpreted as the end of the Abraham Accords’ future prospects.
Israel should be regarded as an essential participant in any serious effort to build a more stable and prosperous Middle East. Sustainable peace requires recognition of Israel’s security concerns, opposition to terrorism, respect for international law, and meaningful diplomacy.
Saudi Arabia has the opportunity to help shape a regional settlement that combines its own security priorities with economic modernization and constructive relations with Israel. Such a development would not erase historical disagreements, but it could create practical incentives for restraint, cooperation, and mutual understanding.
The long-term objective should be clear: a Middle East in which Israel is secure, and cooperation becomes more valuable than continued conflict. The Abraham Accords remain a potential instrument for advancing that vision, provided that the parties demonstrate the political will to turn diplomatic possibilities into practical progress.
The writer is an international affairs analyst and the special envoy for Saudi Arabia for the Global Abrahamic Movement, an NGO dedicated to fostering peace and regional cooperation in the Middle East.

US President Donald Trump has once again suggested that the conflict involving Iran could end soon, renewing attention on the possibility of a diplomatic breakthrough or a further military escalation. The latest comment, highlighted by FinancialJuice, comes as Washington continues to signal confidence in its position while uncertainty persists over the conditions needed to end the fighting.
Trump has repeatedly predicted a swift conclusion to the conflict, but his latest remark does not establish a timetable for ending hostilities. It also provides no new details about an agreement with Tehran, leaving investors and energy traders looking for concrete developments rather than assurances alone.
The conflict has become a major concern for global energy markets because of the risks surrounding oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. The strategic waterway connects the Persian Gulf with international shipping routes, making its security particularly important for oil-producing countries and the economies that depend on their exports.
Trump repeats prediction of a near-term end
Trump has previously said that the United States would win the conflict with Iran “very soon.” On September 28, he told reporters that US officials had spoken with mediators seeking to end the war, although he did not provide details of any progress in negotiations. He also predicted that gasoline prices would fall after the conflict ended.
His latest statement follows a series of similar assurances that the conflict could conclude quickly. However, public predictions about the duration of a war do not necessarily reflect progress in negotiations or a decision to halt military operations.
The central questions remain whether Washington and Tehran can agree on the terms for ending the conflict, what security arrangements would follow and whether both sides would comply with any settlement. Differences over Iran's nuclear programme, sanctions and control of maritime routes have complicated the broader dispute.
A diplomatic resolution could reduce the risk of further attacks and improve confidence in regional trade. Continued military action, by contrast, could prolong uncertainty for shipping operators, energy producers and businesses exposed to higher fuel and transport costs.
Oil prices remain sensitive to developments around Iran
The conflict has placed the Strait of Hormuz at the centre of energy-market concerns. Any sustained disruption to tanker traffic could affect the movement of crude oil and petroleum products, adding pressure to prices and increasing costs for refiners and consumers.
Reuters reported on October 29 that oil prices had eased amid hopes of renewed US-Iran diplomacy, although Brent crude remained near $115 a barrel, roughly $10 above its September average. The report also highlighted continuing uncertainty over negotiations and the possibility of renewed military action.
That market response illustrates the difference between expectations and confirmed changes in supply. Statements suggesting that a conflict may end can ease some concerns, but lasting relief depends on developments that reduce the actual risk to energy production and transportation.
For traders, the key indicators include whether diplomatic talks resume, whether attacks on shipping decline and whether vessels can move safely through major export routes. Insurance costs and freight rates can also reflect the perceived level of danger, even before any direct interruption to oil supplies occurs.
Trump has previously linked an end to the conflict with lower gasoline prices. However, the timing and scale of any decline would also depend on global crude supplies, refining capacity, transportation costs and wider market conditions.
Diplomacy remains uncertain despite optimistic remarks
Trump's repeated predictions have not, on their own, resolved the uncertainty surrounding the conflict. Negotiations would need to address substantive disagreements between the two sides, while any agreement would require mechanisms to ensure that commitments are carried out.
The diplomatic picture remains complicated by the possibility of additional military action and continuing regional security risks. Reports have indicated that the administration is weighing different approaches, including negotiations and further pressure on Iran. The precise outcome and timing remain uncertain.
For global markets, the distinction between a stated intention and an implemented agreement is particularly important. A confirmed ceasefire, a clear negotiating framework or verifiable steps to restore safe shipping would provide stronger evidence of de-escalation than a general prediction that the conflict will end soon.
Investors will therefore be watching for developments that can be independently confirmed, rather than relying on political rhetoric alone. Any sustained improvement in maritime security could ease pressure on energy markets, while renewed attacks or failed negotiations could reverse gains.
For now, Trump's latest comment signals confidence that the conflict will not continue indefinitely, but it does not confirm that an end is imminent. The next decisive developments will be whether diplomatic efforts produce specific commitments and whether conditions on the ground improve enough to reduce the risks facing the region and global energy supplies.

QatarEnergy has stepped up its US LNG purchasing commitments with a new deal with Woodside Energy, following similar agreements with Cheniere, as it seeks to become the world’s largest LNG trader and offset supply disruptions linked to the Strait of Hormuz
The energy giant announced on 29 October that it had signed a long-term sale and purchase agreement (SPA) with Woodside Energy to buy 3M tonnes per annum (mtpa) of LNG from the Louisiana LNG project on the US Gulf Coast, which is currently under construction.
Deliveries are expected to begin in 2030 and continue for 20 years, with the LNG supplied on a free-on-board (FOB) basis.
The agreement follows two long-term SPAs signed with Cheniere last week for the purchase of up to 4 mtpa of LNG from the company’s Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi facilities in Louisiana and Texas, respectively. Deliveries under these agreements are scheduled to begin in 2031 and continue through 2054.
“These additional volumes make QatarEnergy the largest buyer of LNG from the US, and place us in a stronger position to meet the global growing needs for LNG,” Qatar’s Minister of State for Energy Affairs and QatarEnergy president and chief executive Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi said.
“Our Golden Pass LNG project and our expanding portfolio of US LNG purchases reinforce QatarEnergy’s leadership in the LNG industry and support our long-term growth and diversification strategy,” he added.
Mr Al-Kaabi signed the agreement with Woodside Energy chief executive and managing director Liz Westcott.
Qatar targets LNG trading leadership as replacement supply becomes a priority
Commenting on the strategy behind the latest agreements, ICIS LNG analyst Alex Froley told Riviera that Qatar had decided several years ago to expand its operations beyond the country, including through its investment alongside ExxonMobil in the Golden Pass LNG terminal in the US, whose first train began ramping up operations this year.
“However, its diversification plans have taken a step-change following recent events. The company now says it aims to be the biggest LNG trader in the world,” he added.
Mr Froley said the latest agreements were “in line with that ambition.”
Addressing QatarEnergy’s rationale for purchasing LNG volumes from the market, Mr Al-Kaabi said at the Qatar Economic Forum Special Edition in New York that the company had been building one of the world’s largest LNG trading organisations since 2024.
“I would like to mention today that, in the very near future, we will be the largest LNG trader in the world by far. And we’re building our position to become the largest trader,” he added.
In the longer term, Mr Froley believes agreements such as these will give QatarEnergy a larger and more diversified supply portfolio to combine with its global shipping operations and other assets. These include significant capacity bookings at European regasification terminals, which provide additional destinations for its LNG cargoes.
A similar analysis was offered by Energy Flux founder and market analyst Seb Kennedy in a social media post, in which he argued that building a US supply portfolio serves two distinct purposes for QatarEnergy.
The first is to secure replacement supply. “QatarEnergy estimates 12.8 mtpa of capacity at Ras Laffan will be offline for three to five years as it repairs two trains struck by Iran in March. Its trading arm is seeking 2-3 mtpa through 2031 to keep Asian term customers whole, having already used US spot cargoes to bridge the gap. This is short-dated and reactive,” he explained.
Mr Kennedy identified a second purpose: establishing a structural hedge against geopolitical risk.
“The Cheniere volumes are FOB, priced at Henry Hub plus a fixed fee, and don’t start until next decade. Their purpose is permanent: supply that never passes through Hormuz, for an exporter whose entire output sits behind one strait, opposite a belligerent neighbour.”

CAIRO (AP) — A Saudi airstrike in western Taiz killed at least 13 people on Thursday, the Houthi-run health ministry said, as local officials said a siege of the Yemeni city by Houthi rebels has pushed residents into famine.
“The city is in famine, not on the brink of it,” Taiz Gov. Nabil Shamsan said in a briefing, adding that he was speaking a mile away from the front line.
“The Houthis cannot use the siege of Taiz to justify the humanitarian catastrophe they are causing civilians,” said Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher for Human Rights Watch.
The group said Thursday that the siege, which started in early October, could amount to the war crime of using starvation as a method of warfare.
Shamsan said the city, which hosts about 1 million people, now receives only a fraction of the water it needs after Houthi forces seized its last outside source. Cooking gas has been blocked entirely, forcing restaurants to close and families to burn wood, while hospitals have nearly run out of oxygen to supply to patients.
The World Food Program said it could not reach over 600,000 people in Taiz who depend on humanitarian aid, and that wheat flour stocks were nearly exhausted. Shamsan said 271 people have been killed and 1,129 wounded since the offensive began earlier this month.
“Even those who could be rescued, they shell them or hit the ambulance with snipers. We’ve had to use a civilian car as an ambulance - they hit that too,” Shamsan said.
Houthi leader Abdul Malik al-Houthi on Thursday dismissed reports of a siege as “Saudi-fabricated claims.”
“As far as food and humanitarian needs are concerned, the way is open,” he said in a televised speech on the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV, adding that his forces were only cutting off weapons supplies to what he called “Saudi-backed militias.”
The pressure is compounded by people fleeing the fighting elsewhere. Taiz has taken about 124,000 displaced people since August, according to the U.N. migration agency.
Yemen descended into civil war in 2014, when the Houthis seized much of the country’s north, including the capital, Sanaa, and forced the internationally recognized government into exile.
Taiz has been a focal point of fighting ever since, with government forces holding the city center while the Houthis control the surrounding roads.

Look east, and the playbook is changing too. Baghdad’s $17-billion Development Road would link Grand Faw Port to Turkey and Europe. Washington likes Iraq diversifying away from Tehran, but it isn’t writing a blank check. (See my post: Iraqi Maritime Line Returns to Gulf Shipping After 50 Years https://www.inboundlogistics.com/articles/iraqi-maritime-line-resumes-gulf-shipping/)
The administration enforces strict secondary sanctions on players like Iraq’s International Development Bank. The message: if you want international capital for rail and port megaprojects, your banking rails better be clean. Every transaction needs an OFAC check for Iranian ties.
Are We Making Progress?
It seems so. Two models are taking shape.
The Mediterranean Bypass: Syria is becoming a viable, direct Levantine feeder option.
The Guardrailed Inland Route: Iraq offers massive transit potential, but compliance friction will dictate the pace.
UN meetings and White House visits used to sit in the background of logistics. Today, they’re the route planner. Smart operators aren’t just checking berth depth or rail mileage; they’re reading Treasury press releases before making long-term supply chain decisions.

articles.title: Trump tells allies to brace for return to Iran war after midterms
articles.summary: U.S. officials have warned several Middle Eastern countries and regional allies to prepare for possible renewed military action against Iran after next week’s U.S. midterm election...
articles.full_text:
U.S. officials have warned several Middle Eastern countries and regional allies to prepare for possible renewed military action against Iran after next week’s U.S. midterm elections and potential Iranian retaliation, according to two diplomats briefed on the matter.
Both of the diplomats spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment about the sensitive warnings conveyed by U.S. diplomats and defense officials.
President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on whether to carry out new strikes against Iran, the diplomats stressed. The president, however, has repeatedly said that he is weighing ordering new military action once the critical Nov. 3 elections in the United States are over.
Those threats and the fresh U.S. urgings for allies to prepare for potential retaliation are putting the region on alert that a return to major operations could now be on the horizon.
The White House and U.S. officials declined to comment.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran "continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed" and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month – summarily rejected by Trump – that the Iranians still want to see used as the basis to return to a cease-fire.
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates Foreign Ministry issued a statement urging the sides to "exercise wisdom and pursue political solutions to help contain tensions" and prevent a return to full-scale operations in the war that began in late February.
The U.S. has told regional allies that the new round of military action could last for several days, but regional officials are bracing for Iran and its proxy groups to retaliate – leading to a fight that could last even longer, the diplomats said.
The allies have also been urged by U.S. officials to take precautionary measures in anticipation that Iran's response will include retaliatory strikes on energy facilities and other crucial infrastructure.
While the U.S. has not carried out a strike against Iran since early September, the situation in the Middle East has become more complicated.
The conflict has spread, with Iran-backed Houthi rebels carrying out attacks on Saudi Arabia’s oil infrastructure and airports. A Saudi-led coalition has responded with its own deadly attacks on Houthi-held territory in Yemen.
The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Gulf nations being briefed to be prepared for potential escalation by the U.S.
It's unclear how soon after Election Day that the U.S. military would be ready to potentially resume strikes.
The Pentagon late last month deployed the USS Theodore Roosevelt, along with a series of amphibious landing ships with Marines aboard – roughly 9,000 troops in all – from San Diego to the Persian Gulf to bolster the U.S. military in the region.
At the time, one U.S. official said this deployment could lead to an unusually high naval presence of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines, as well as hundreds of aircraft, in the region, which has only occurred a handful of times in the last two decades. The Navy had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003.
Late Wednesday, reports emerged that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had fired the Pentagon’s top military planner. Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was removed as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff, according to a defense official who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel matters. That official said there is no immediate replacement for Sylvia and no reason has been given for the firing.
Trump, who has focused in recent weeks on campaigning for Republicans ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, has been evasive about what he plans to do next with Iran.
The war has proved to be a heavy weight on Republican candidates as they make their case to voters who are fatigued by rising gasoline prices, a byproduct of the war that's driven up costs across nearly every sector in the global economy.
The cost of fighting the Iran war to American taxpayers has grown to $47.1 billion, according to the latest estimate the Pentagon has provided to Congress.
While campaigning for Republicans, Trump has consistently assured voters that the war’s end is near, while also threatening that a new round of bombing could be coming once the election passes.
During a campaign stop in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday, Trump said a conclusive end to the eight-month-old conflict could be coming "in a couple of weeks, if you don’t mind."
"Somebody asked me before, when will the war in Iran end?" Trump said earlier in the same address. "I said, ‘Whenever I want it to end.’ It’ll be very quick, but we have to have it end properly, with total and complete – a total statement, they will never have a nuclear weapon."
Trump may be looking at a postelection timeline for possible action, but the region is on edge that Tehran could do something provocative before then – especially if they feel U.S. actions is imminent, said Jonathan Schanzer, executive director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington think tank.
"Why would they wait until after the elections here ... if they could initiate it and potentially gain the upper hand?" he said.

articles.title: Qatar and Sweden conclude second round of bilateral investment treaty in Doha - The Peninsula Qatar
articles.summary: Qatar and Sweden conclude second round of bilateral investment treaty in Doha  The Peninsula Qatar
articles.full_text:
Sweden’s Chief Negotiator for Investment Treaties at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, H E Ambassador Magnus Hartog-Holm
Doha, Qatar: Qatar and Sweden concluded a second round of negotiations on a bilateral investment treaty in Doha, marking progress in efforts to strengthen economic ties and create a more predictable environment for investors, an official has said.
In an exclusive interview with The Peninsula, Sweden’s Chief Negotiator for Investment Treaties at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, H E Ambassador Magnus Hartog-Holm, said the negotiations had advanced during his visit to Doha and that both sides looked forward to making further progress in the coming months.
“The next step is to turn this momentum into concrete opportunities by bringing investors, companies and institutions closer together,” Ambassador Hartog-Holm said at the UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) World Investment Forum 2026.
He noted that Sweden and Qatar had complementary strengths in industry, innovation and technology that could support deeper cooperation and long-term partnerships.
The Ambassador identified artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, and energy technologies as areas with potential for greater Qatari investment in Sweden.
He said Sweden’s innovation ecosystem and stable, predictable business environment could complement Qatar’s expertise in energy and its ambitions to diversify its economy.
“These areas offer potential not only for investment but also for industrial cooperation and joint development,” he said.
The official stressed that the objective should be to combine the countries’ respective strengths to generate long-term value for both economies.
Closer cooperation in technology and advanced industries could provide opportunities for companies to expand their international reach while developing new products and solutions, he said.
Beyond the bilateral negotiations, Ambassador Hartog-Holm said Sweden utilised the World Investment Forum to contribute to discussions on reforming the international investment framework.
“While these agreements remain important for protecting and promoting investment, they must also reflect the evolving responsibilities of governments,” he said.
Sweden is working to modernise its bilateral investment treaties by introducing provisions covering sustainable development, transparency, corporate social responsibility and states’ right to regulate in the public interest.
Ambassador Hartog-Holm said investor protection and governments’ ability to regulate should be treated as complementary objectives rather than competing priorities.
“Investors need legal certainty and a predictable business environment, while governments must retain the flexibility to pursue legitimate public policy objectives, including climate action, public health and sustainable development,” he said.
He stated that Sweden’s approach was shaped by its legal and policy commitments as a member of the European Union.
Ambassador Hartog-Holm added international cooperation was essential to building a more predictable, sustainable and development-oriented investment system, but stressed that governments also needed to take responsibility for reviewing their own agreements.
The Ambassador also underscored that Sweden supports reform initiatives within UNCTAD, the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL), the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and the European Union, while pursuing a long-term programme to modernise its bilateral investment treaties.
He welcomed UNCTAD’s new Guiding Principles for International Investment Agreement (IIA) Reform, describing them as useful guidance for countries seeking to reconcile investment protection with contemporary development priorities.

articles.title: Port of NEOM, Ceva Almajdouie partner on Europe-GCC-Iraq trade corridor - Food Business Middle East & Africa
articles.summary: Port of NEOM, Ceva Almajdouie partner on Europe-GCC-Iraq trade corridor  Food Business Middle East & Africa
articles.full_text:
The port’s connectivity across the Europe-Egypt-Saudi Arabia-GCC-Iraq corridor is intended to support regional trade, strengthen supply chain resilience and enable more flexible cargo routing.
SAUDI ARABIA – The Port of NEOM has signed an agreement with Ceva Almajdouie Logistics to explore integrated logistics solutions linking Europe, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the GCC, and Iraq via a multimodal trade corridor, according to a joint statement.
Located within Oxagon, the Port of NEOM is becoming a multimodal logistics hub that links international shipping routes to inland markets across Saudi Arabia and the wider region.
Partner capabilities and corridor scope
The Port of NEOM is part of NEOM, the US$500 billion Saudi futuristic city project, with Oxagon positioned as an industrial and logistics center on the Red Sea coast.
Ceva Almajdouie Logistics is a joint venture between CMA CGM’s Ceva Logistics and Saudi-based Almajdouie Holding, providing transport, customs clearance, warehousing and cross-border operations across the Kingdom.
The agreement aims to enhance end-to-end cargo transport by integrating maritime connectivity with inland transport, customs brokerage, warehousing and cross-border logistics services.
Integration model and market implications
Under the proposed collaboration, the Port of NEOM will leverage its Red Sea location and multimodal connectivity, while Ceva Almajdouie contributes logistics capabilities beyond the port gate.
The two companies will explore integrated supply chain solutions that cover different cargo types and connect sea freight with inland distribution networks.
Cargo bound for Iraq, Jordan and northern Saudi Arabia currently moves through Jeddah, King Abdullah Port or Gulf gateways inside the Strait of Hormuz. A NEOM corridor offers an alternative that avoids Hormuz entirely, a route that has become more relevant as regional tensions disrupt Gulf routing.
The partnership also positions NEOM to capture transhipment and distribution volumes from Egypt, where ports at Sokhna and Alexandria serve as Mediterranean gateways.
Additionally, linking Egypt’s Mediterranean gateways to a Red Sea corridor would create an Asia-Europe route that bypasses both Hormuz and the southern approach to the Suez Canal.
For Ceva Almajdouie, the agreement secures access to a port under development that will eventually handle substantial container volumes, giving the logistics provider an early foothold as the facility builds its cargo base.

articles.title: Marriage Of Convenience: Russia And Iran Deepen Trade Ties, But Their Partnership Has Limits - Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty
articles.summary: Marriage Of Convenience: Russia And Iran Deepen Trade Ties, But Their Partnership Has Limits  Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty
articles.full_text:
It is said that politics makes strange bedfellows. Apparently international sanctions do too.
Russia and Iran, the world's two most-sanctioned nations, are deepening trade and financial ties to reduce their reliance on Western-dominated economic systems, a marriage of convenience through national currencies, direct banking links, and alternative transport routes.
This deepening economic cooperation is perhaps most visible in the Caspian Sea, where shipping activity between Russia and Iran has increased as Moscow's war in Ukraine and Middle East tensions disrupt established trade routes.
According to data from Castellum, a global risk adviser, Russia is now the most-sanctioned nation in the world with more than 5,000 international actions against it, followed by Iran with some 3,600 designations.
"Russia's invasion of Ukraine and Iran's destabilization have simultaneously spotlighted Eurasia's strategic importance while testing the limits of the region's historic alignments," Tina Dolbaia and Leah Kieff of the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said recently.
Officially recorded bilateral trade between the two nations relies heavily on agricultural commodities: Russia exports grain and vegetable oils to Iran, while Tehran supplies fruits and vegetables in return.
Moscow's exports also encompass heavy industrial goods, including metals, timber, and machinery.
But beyond this transparent commercial exchange, the economic relationship contains a strategic military component.
According to the independent London-based maritime intelligence provider Lloyd's List Intelligence, the number of active Russian- and Iranian-flagged vessels operating in the Caspian rose 21 percent year on year in August.
The increase began in March, following US and Israeli strikes on Iran that started on February 28 and disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. A US maritime blockade imposed in April further complicated Iranian shipping routes.
"The cargoes being transported are often difficult to identify," Lloyd's List reported, noting that trade data points to an increasing role for agricultural commodities.
Regional analyst Nitya Labh, who has written about the growth of Russia's and Iran's shadow fleets, points out that what began as an ad hoc practice involving a small handful of isolated nations has evolved into a massive, highly sophisticated global network.
"Today, estimates suggest the shadow fleet is over 1,300 vessels, accounting for at least one in every five oil tankers worldwide," Labh told RFE/RL.
Trade Has Grown Substantially
Russia's ambassador to Iran said in June that bilateral trade reached about $5.8 billion in 2025, up 21 percent from the previous year.
ProZerno, a Russian grain consultancy, reported that Iran imported 1.7 million tons of Russian wheat from July 2025 to January 2026, compared with 565,000 tons in the previous agricultural year.
Dolbaia, an associate fellow at CSIS, said agricultural products and foodstuffs dominate officially recorded trade. But the relationship also has a less transparent dimension involving military-related goods and efforts to limit exposure to Western sanctions.
Iran supplied Russia with attack drones early in Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but Russia has since localized and improved production, the expert said.
She added that there have been reports of Russia sending drone components to Iran via the Caspian Sea.
Alternative Payments
The two countries are also trying to make payments without relying on Western financial channels.
They have expanded settlement in rubles and rials and connected their respective interbank financial messaging systems, allowing banks to communicate allowing banks to communicate without using SWIFT, the international network banks use to exchange payment instructions.
A CSIS report co-authored by Dolbaia in April identified the International North-South Transport Corridor as a central element of that strategy.
The planned road, rail, and maritime network would connect Russia with Iran and extend toward the Persian Gulf and India through the South Caucasus and Central Asia, although major infrastructure and geopolitical obstacles remain.
More Trade, Harder To Track
Lloyd's List Intelligence found that the number of active general cargo ships on the Caspian route rose from 105 in February to 215 in August. The segment recorded a 36 percent year-on-year increase in carrying capacity, according to the report.
But the corridor cannot easily absorb the volume of trade handled by major maritime routes.
Ships are constrained by the Volga-Don river system, shallow water, declining water levels, limited port capacity, and rail bottlenecks.
Tanker activity has increased from a very low base. Three Russian-flagged crude-oil tankers were recorded on the route in August.
Lloyd's List said all three switched off their Automatic Identification System (AIS) signals as they approached Russian and Iranian ports, then reappeared during transit, obscuring the visibility of their cargo movements.
Ships are not required to keep AIS switched on in all circumstances, making activity in the Caspian difficult to track.
The CSIS researchers argue that sanctions evasion is one of the drivers behind the countries' efforts to develop alternative trade infrastructure. But the existence of a new route, or a vessel going dark on its tracking system, does not by itself prove that a specific shipment is illicit.
Allegations of military transfers through the Caspian have added to scrutiny.
Kyiv has accused Moscow of using the route to funnel military equipment.
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) reported that Ukraine targeted several sanctioned cargo vessels in the sea following assessments that they were transporting military cargo.
ISW analysis also notes that the covert route has been utilized to shift sensitive defense assets, drone components, and ammunition.
Lloyd's List said the allegations remain unconfirmed, and neither government has publicly acknowledged such transfers.
While the European Union expanded its enforcement in 2026 by passing its 20th sanctions package to target shadow fleet owners, managers, and service providers, physical interdictions carry severe military risks, regional expert Labh warns.
Labh cited the risks of maritime enforcement, pointing to a May 2025 incident in which a Russian Su-35 briefly entered Estonian airspace as Estonia attempted to stop a suspected Russian shadow-fleet tanker.
In August 2026, Russia President Vladimir Putin separately threatened retaliation for Western seizures of Russian commercial vessels, calling them "piracy."
But despite the growing bilateral trade, Dolbaia cautioned against overstating what Iran can do for Russia.
"For Russia, cooperation with China is far more important to withstand Western sanctions effects than cooperation with Iran," she told RFE/RL, noting that China buys Russian energy and supplies components used in Russia's defense sector.
Russia's trade with China surpasses $200 billion annually, dwarfing the single-digit billions traded with Iran.
