articles.title: Iran war costs US taxpayers $47.1 billion
articles.summary: The U.S. war with Iran has cost American taxpayers an estimated $47.1 billion, according to new Pentagon figures submitted to Congress, as the conflict's financial toll fuels debat...
articles.full_text:
The U.S. war with Iran has cost American taxpayers an estimated $47.1 billion, according to new Pentagon figures submitted to Congress, as the conflict's financial toll fuels debate ahead of the midterm elections and President Donald Trump signals that further military action remains possible.
The figure from U.S. Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, is as of Oct. 16 and offers the most up-to-date cost for the conflict since it was launched in late February by the United States and Israel. The latest price tag, obtained by The Associated Press this week, shows a $3.5 billion bump in U.S. spending since early September, when that figure stood at about $43.6 billion.
The growing cost of the unpopular war and its economic ripple effects on energy prices could hurt Republicans in next week's midterm elections. Voters on Tuesday will decide which political party controls Congress during Trump's last two years in office.
The Republican president has said new strikes on Iran are an option after the midterms and is sending more military resources to the Middle East, despite initially promising Americans a military campaign that would last only a matter of weeks. As the war’s costs in lives, tax dollars and economic impact grow, most voters say they want Congress to prioritize ending the conflict, according to a recent AP-NORC poll.
The expense of the conflict and military spending in general are already a contentious issue on Capitol Hill, where the Trump administration is pushing for the passage of a historic $1.5 trillion military budget proposal. The White House is also asking lawmakers to approve a $95 billion package that would help fund the Iran war and other priorities.
Wednesday marks eight months of the war, which Democrats have been trying to end through legislation that has failed to pass the Republican-controlled Congress.
"Trump and his ego led us into this war with no plan, no authority, and no exit strategy," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said in a news release. "Senate Democrats will continue to do everything in our power to end this disaster of a war and stop the costs, chaos, and corruption seeping from the White House.”
In the latest estimate, the bulk of the war's costs are for replacing munitions, at about $29 billion. The advanced weapons most in demand and whose stockpiles have been drawn down are defensive missile interceptors, such as those launched by the Army’s Patriot and THAAD systems, with a single Patriot interceptor costing millions of dollars.
The Pentagon says about $11.9 billion is related to costs of operations, while an additional $6 billion is tied to equipment losses. The Air Force's costs are now $7.6 billion, and the Army's are more than $2 billion. The Navy's costs were listed at $1.45 billion, which is a significant drop from the $2.2 billion listed in early September.
When asked why the Navy’s cost estimates decreased over the roughly six-week period, both the Navy and U.S. Central Command referred the questions to the Pentagon, which did not immediately respond to emails requesting comment on the new cost estimates.
The latest estimate does not include damage to U.S. bases in the Middle East, which the Islamic Republic has attacked with ballistic missiles and drones. A report from the Pentagon inspector general released last month said Iranian strikes have damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.
The Pentagon’s official tally lists 21 service members killed and 865 wounded in the conflict. That count includes troops who died in medical events and other situations that do not have a direct connection to the conflict, with 18 service members having been killed from Iranian strikes, combat aircraft crashes or the disposal of Iranian drones.
While Trump has mused repeatedly about whether to make a deal with Iran or "finish them off,” a third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are making their way to the region. The Trump administration also has reduced staffing at some U.S. Embassies after receiving intelligence that Iran has stepped up efforts to target American personnel.

articles.title: 'Lesser of 2 evils': Israel's election leaves Gaza future in limbo
articles.summary: In Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip, where Israeli airstrikes remain a regular occurrence despite a cease-fire, residents were closely following Israel’s election results, h...
articles.full_text:
In Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip, where Israeli airstrikes remain a regular occurrence despite a cease-fire, residents were closely following Israel’s election results, hoping that anyone but Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would lead the next government.
“All of their policies toward Gaza are tough, but we choose the lesser of two evils,” resident Ayman Ahmed said.
Ahmed said he hoped Netanyahu’s main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, would prevail, adding that he supported U.S. President Donald Trump’s roadmap for Gaza.
The plan calls for disarming Hamas and installing a new U.S.-backed government. It also requires Israel to withdraw its forces from the territory and allow reconstruction to begin.
Most of Gaza’s 2 million people remain displaced, living in the bombed-out ruins of their former homes or in squalid tent camps.
Netanyahu agreed to Trump’s plan but never implemented it beyond the initial stage, which involved a partial withdrawal and increased aid in exchange for the return of the remaining hostages held by Hamas, both living and dead.
The plan has been largely frozen for nearly a year.
In the rubble-strewn streets near Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, Mohammed Abed said a Netanyahu victory would be seen as a triumph for his agenda but that he did not expect major changes regardless of who took power.
Eisenkot, a former military chief, favors tough responses to “Israel’s enemies.”
“An Eisenkot victory will not dramatically change the situation, because their policies are almost similar,” Abed said. “In the end, it will be the same.”
Underscoring Abed’s pessimism, two strikes in Khan Younis on Wednesday killed one man and wounded at least six others, according to health officials at Nasser Hospital. Israel’s military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
More than 1,550 Palestinians in Gaza have been killed by the Israeli military since the cease-fire between Israel and Hamas began in October 2025, according to the blockaded Palestinian enclave’s Health Ministry.
The ministry says women and children account for roughly half of those killed.
The Gaza genocide began following Hamas' incursion into southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, which killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages.
Israel’s retaliatory offensive killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and destroyed much of Gaza.
Hasan al-Masri, who was displaced from his home in Beit Hanoun in northern Gaza, said he desperately hoped the election would bring change to the territory.
“We pray to God that these elections bring a positive outcome for us,” he said. “We have been utterly devastated; nothing remains. They have killed our children, destroyed our homes, and everything we had is gone.”
The future of Gaza was barely discussed during Israel’s election campaign. The only major candidate to advocate for a two-state solution was Yair Golan, head of the small Democrats party.
Asked whether the prospect of a future Palestinian state was something Gaza residents hoped for, Ahmed said, “only people outside Gaza care about these topics,” adding that their main concern was finding enough food to eat.
He said he feared a Netanyahu victory would bring more war and suffering.
“We support any effort to bring down Netanyahu,” he said.

articles.title: Netanyahu likely to win most seats in Israeli polls: What happens next?
articles.summary: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies appear on track ​to win the most seats in Israel's parliament after an election this week, though neither he nor his ⁠main competit...
articles.full_text:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies appear on track to win the most seats in Israel's parliament after an election this week, though neither he nor his main competitor, Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a majority.
Votes are now being tallied, followed by potentially long negotiations as parties try to assemble a governing coalition. If those talks fail, Israel could head to another round of elections.
Israel's Central Election Committee was tallying votes on Wednesday, and it will likely take until Thursday before definitive results of the election are known.
The committee will also tally hundreds of thousands of ballots by Israeli soldiers, as well as diplomats, who voted from outside the country.
The committee's tallying followed exit polls from major Israeli TV channels. Those polls can help give a general sense of each party’s relative strength but are not considered a reliable barometer of precise results, particularly in Israel’s fragmented political system.
The final vote tally is expected by Oct. 30 and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on Nov. 4.
Knesset seats are allocated by proportional representation to national party lists, with parties needing to pass a threshold of 3.25% of the national vote to secure seats.
About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time.
After the final tally is in, President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders on whom they want as prime minister and then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.
That nominee has up to 42 days to form a government.
No single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, so governments are formed by a coalition of parties, and negotiations on forming a government often take weeks. Every Knesset seat counts and small parties can have a big impact by becoming kingmakers.
If the nominee fails, others can get a chance to try. If no government emerges, another election is called, with the present Cabinet staying on as a caretaker government.

articles.title: Netanyahu bloc leads Israeli polls after 50% of votes counted: Committee
articles.summary: The camp of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was ahead of the opposition on Wednesday after 50% of votes were counted in Israel's pivotal general election, figures from the Centra...
articles.full_text:
The camp of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was ahead of the opposition on Wednesday after 50% of votes were counted in Israel's pivotal general election, figures from the Central Elections Committee showed.
After 50.1% of ballots were counted, Netanyahu's bloc was projected to win 56 of the 120 seats in the parliament, compared with 49 for the opposition bloc and 15 for the Arab parties. The partial results are likely to change, and several exit polls showed the camps neck-and-neck without a majority.

articles.title: Netanyahu, Eisenkot deadlocked as Israel election delivers no clear winner
articles.summary: Israel’s election has left Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition challenger Gadi Eisenkot without a clear path to power, as exit polls showed their blocs deadlocked desp...
articles.full_text:
Israel’s election has left Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition challenger Gadi Eisenkot without a clear path to power, as exit polls showed their blocs deadlocked despite record turnout and significant gains by Arab Israeli parties.
Eisenkot, a 66-year-old former military chief, vowed Wednesday to move quickly to form a government, saying voters had rejected Netanyahu’s divisive leadership.
Netanyahu, meanwhile, called for a strong right-wing government and highlighted the prospect of renewed military action against Iran alongside U.S. President Donald Trump.
Neither leader claimed victory. Exit polls from Israel’s three major television networks showed the competing blocs close to evenly matched, with neither securing the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Kan 11 and Channel 13 projected a 51-51 tie, while Channel 12 gave Netanyahu’s Likud-led bloc a narrow 52-49 advantage. Final results were expected Thursday or Friday, leaving the country facing potentially prolonged coalition negotiations or another election.
Speaking to supporters in Tel Aviv, Eisenkot said the public had delivered a vote of no confidence in Netanyahu and urged the longtime prime minister to retire from politics.
“The public has voted for change,” Eisenkot said. “A worthy leader would accept the people’s vote of no confidence and announce his retirement from political life today.”
He also warned Netanyahu against using national security to advance his political interests, raising concerns about the prospect of renewed military action against Iran while the government’s future remained uncertain.
“Netanyahu, don’t you dare use Israel’s security for your political needs,” Eisenkot said.
Netanyahu did not immediately address supporters after the initial projections. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, an ally of the prime minister, dismissed the opposition’s victory claims as premature.
Arab Israeli parties made some of the strongest gains, with exit polls projecting a combined 17 to 18 seats. Their increased representation could prove decisive in determining whether Netanyahu’s coalition returns to power.
Turnout reached 77.7%, according to Israel’s Central Elections Committee, the highest in more than two decades and about 7 percentage points above the 2022 election.
The strong participation included a surge among Palestinian citizens of Israel, many of whom voted to prevent Netanyahu’s nationalist-religious coalition from returning to government.
At the headquarters of the Joint List, an alliance of Arab parties, supporters celebrated as exit polls were released. Faten Gattas, a candidate for the alliance, pledged continued opposition to occupation and racism.
“We refuse the occupation and racism, and we will remain here,” she said in Nazareth.
Mansour Abbas, a prominent Arab Israeli political leader, said the right-wing camp had suffered a major defeat and indicated he was open to working with Eisenkot.
However, Eisenkot has largely ruled out forming a government with Arab lawmakers, complicating his route to power. Their parties could still support a minority government in parliamentary votes without formally joining a coalition.
Far-right leader Itamar Ben Gvir warned Netanyahu against forming a unity government with Eisenkot, calling such a move a mistake. Ben Gvir, a prominent supporter of Jewish settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank, and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich were projected to win a combined 13 seats, short of the gains some had expected.
Gideon Rahat, a political scientist at Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said Ben Gvir’s polarizing campaign had helped mobilize Arab Israeli voters.
“Even if Netanyahu lost, that doesn’t mean Eisenkot won,” Rahat said.
The election was held in the shadow of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas incursion, which killed about 1,200 people in Israel and saw 251 others taken hostage, according to Israeli figures.
The attack triggered the Gaza genocide and wider regional conflicts involving Hezbollah in Lebanon and Iran.
Netanyahu campaigned on his security record, arguing that Israeli military operations against Hamas, Hezbollah and Iranian targets had made the country safer. He also emphasized his relationship with Trump as an opportunity to confront Iran.
Addressing Likud supporters in Jerusalem early Wednesday, Netanyahu said Israel faced a historic opportunity to eliminate what he described as the Iranian threat.
“Israel faces a singular historical opportunity, together with our partner President Trump, to remove the existential threat of Iran once and for all,” he said.
Eisenkot, who joined Netanyahu’s wartime government after the Hamas attack before resigning about eight months later, challenged the prime minister’s authority to make major security decisions without a clear public mandate.
He urged the security establishment to resist attempts to put political interests ahead of national security.
Despite presenting himself as a centrist on domestic politics, Eisenkot maintains a hawkish position on Palestinian issues. He opposes Palestinian statehood and says Hamas’ military wing must be destroyed or dismantled.
He has described Israel’s campaign in Gaza as a failure because Hamas remains in control. Gaza health authorities have reported more than 74,000 Palestinian deaths during the war.
The exit polls suggested a major setback for Netanyahu’s nationalist-religious coalition, which once held 68 seats but appeared far short of a majority.
Netanyahu, 77, has served as prime minister for nearly 19 years across several terms and has repeatedly survived political crises. After four inconclusive elections in two years, his opponents briefly removed him from office in 2021. He returned to power in December 2022.
His latest campaign included sharp attacks on Arab Israeli voters. Netanyahu accused them of trying to “steal the election,” while his Likud party unsuccessfully sought to keep polling stations open beyond their scheduled 10:00 p.m. closing time.
The opposition accused him of seeking grounds to challenge the results. Netanyahu also alleged that three senior officials from the United Arab List had been arrested in southern Israel with envelopes of cash. Election authorities described the incident as an isolated local case.
Netanyahu entered the election facing criticism over intelligence failures that allowed the Oct. 7 attack and longstanding corruption charges, which he denies. He also faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant related to the Gaza war.
His government’s policies have deepened Israel’s international isolation amid the war in Gaza, expanding settlements and violence in the occupied West Bank.
Eisenkot, meanwhile, has drawn public sympathy after losing his son Gal, who was killed fighting in Gaza, and two nephews during the war. Before voting, he privately visited his son’s grave.
The son of working-class Moroccan Jewish immigrants, Eisenkot would become Israel’s first prime minister of Middle Eastern or North African descent if he forms a government.
The election’s outcome remains uncertain as votes are counted and smaller parties prepare to negotiate their role in the next government.
Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute, described the exit polls as a major blow to Netanyahu’s coalition but cautioned that Eisenkot had not emerged as a clear winner.
The deadlock could allow Netanyahu to remain caretaker prime minister during lengthy negotiations. If neither camp can assemble a governing majority, another election may be necessary.
Some Israelis returned from abroad to vote. Eilana Zisblit, 55, who has lived in Canada for nearly three decades, traveled to Israel to support a center-right party in Eisenkot’s bloc.
“The country is going in a really, really bad direction,” she told Agence France-Presse (AFP), saying the situation affected Jews and Arabs in Israel as well as Jews abroad.
Eisenkot has urged political leaders to avoid another election, arguing that the record turnout demonstrated the public’s desire for change.

articles.title: Iran leaves JD Vance's message unanswered, security source says

articles.full_text:
Tehran has yet to respond to a message sent by U.S. Vice President JD Vance to Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei, a senior Iranian security source said Thursday.
The source told Iran’s semi-official Fars News Agency that Vance sent a message to Rezaei but said Tehran had not yet responded.
The official dismissed media speculation about the contents of the message, saying the reports were inaccurate.
The source said correspondence between American and Iranian officials was not unusual, noting that exchanges had taken place on several occasions, including during the tenure of former U.S. President Barack Obama.
The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Vance sent a letter to Rezaei to revive peace negotiations.
Citing American officials and people familiar with the matter, the newspaper said the letter was sent at President Donald Trump’s direction as Washington explored whether a diplomatic framework could prevent renewed U.S. military strikes against Iran.
Trump denied directing Vance to initiate negotiations, however, saying the communication concerned Iran’s need for medical supplies.
"No, what it is, is that they need help with medical supplies and various things,” Trump said when asked whether he had directed Vance to contact Iran.
The diplomatic efforts come amid continued tensions between Washington and Tehran about implementing a June memorandum of understanding and navigating the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Israel on edge over final election results as uncertainty looms
articles.summary: Israelis awaited final election results Thursday amid indications that neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies nor opposition parties, including Arab-led factions,...
articles.full_text:
Israelis awaited final election results Thursday amid indications that neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies nor opposition parties, including Arab-led factions, had secured a parliamentary majority.
Adding to the uncertainty, the head of the Central Elections Committee asked the Shin Bet intelligence service to investigate alleged foreign interference. The letter dated Wednesday noted alleged funding by "foreign entities against the Israeli interest," without specifics, and could not speak to the validity of the claims. It was not clear who made them. It requested findings within the week. Israeli law requires election results to be certified by Nov. 4.
Netanyahu swiftly seized on the request to the Shin Bet to assert that no party should cooperate with Arab-led ones, even though the letter said nothing about that issue. His chief rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, warned that political actors should not "exploit the situation" to influence the timing of the swearing-in of the next parliament, set for Nov. 10.
Yair Golan, head of the Democrats party, accused Netanyahu of "attempting to undermine the election results through an ugly delegitimization campaign directed against the will of the public – and against the Arab public in particular."
Sami Abu Shehadeh, chair of a party on the Arab-led Joint List, called the claims a new phase of "incitement" against Arab-led groups.
The developments amplified the difficult decisions for the weeks ahead. Those include whether some Jewish and Arab parties would team up in a historic alliance, or whether some parties that campaigned on ousting Netanyahu would toss that aside and join forces with the deeply divisive prime minister.
While this plays out, Netanyahu remains in charge.
Final results could come as early as Thursday evening after about a half-million absentee ballots are counted from military personnel, diplomats, people in prisons and hospitals, and others. They are not expected to sway the results dramatically.
Local media projected 53 parliament seats for Netanyahu's bloc, 48 seats for opposition parties and 19 for Arab-led ones, which also want Netanyahu out.
Netanyahu's Likud, despite receiving the most votes, earlier accused Arab-led parties of stealing the election and asked the election committee to investigate. It did not provide specific evidence to support its claims. The election committee has said the number of reported irregularities in the relatively calm election was low.
Even without a role in a coalition, Arab-led parties could assert their growing power by supporting other Netanyahu opponents in the next parliament, the Knesset. That could include electing a new speaker, giving them control of the agenda and potentially allowing them to advance and pass legislation before a new government is formed.
Eisenkot has indicated he is open, with conditions, to joining forces with the Arab-led parties that had a strong showing, as some Arab citizens broke longstanding vows never to vote in a country where they have long faced discrimination. Such an alliance would reach the 61-seat majority needed to control the 120-seat Knesset.
Ahmad Tibi, second on the Arab-led Joint List, told Army Radio he’s heard from the opposition bloc to discuss replacing the Knesset speaker and he told them the party would support the bloc’s candidate. He also urged Eisenkot to have political courage.
The Joint List has noted the "unprecedented show of strength" by Arab voters and the Jewish voters "willing to swim against the tide of racism."
There were small rallies overnight in Tel Aviv and in far more conservative Jerusalem, in support of a coalition that includes Arab-led parties. Until 2021, no Arab party had joined a coalition government and that was brief.
Next week, Israel’s president will task someone with forming the next government. It has traditionally been the leader of the party with the most votes, but that’s not required.
If a new government cannot be formed after multiple attempts, Israel would face a new election early next year. On Wednesday, President Isaac Herzog signaled he wanted to avoid that step – something Eisenkot has said as well.
New elections bring new questions, including whether Arab citizens would again go to the polls in large numbers and whether the tens of thousands of Israelis who flew home to vote would do it again. Many had said they took that step to save the country from Netanyahu.
Israel, already divided along multiple fault lines – Jews and Arabs, secular and religious – entered the election with huge and painful issues at stake.
Those include whether the fast-growing ultra-Orthodox population should remain exempted from compulsory military service in a country where many families have seen their sons and daughters killed in three years of inconclusive wars.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, has been especially polarizing, with corruption allegations hanging over him along with accusations that he delayed making deals over the war in Gaza, including to free hostages, for political gain.
While many Israelis voted with security issues first in mind, the country’s international standing is also at stake after widespread criticism over the treatment of Palestinians in Gaza and growing violence by Jewish settlers in the occupied West Bank .
For Arab citizens, who make up 20% of Israel’s population, there is cautious hope of change. "God willing, we will have something for us in the government, something that will bring us our rights," said Brosli Elias, a resident of Nazareth, one of Israel’s largest Arab cities.
Meanwhile, the threat of further strikes against Iran adds to the election uncertainty, as the Trump administration has spoken of new attacks after the midterm elections on Nov. 3. Experts have said Netanyahu could seize on a renewed all-out war to press for a unity government with him in charge.
That could delay what Netanyahu has long resisted: a public inquiry into the security failures into Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas incursion that sparked Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.

articles.title: Merz seeks swift end to Iran war amid mounting pressure on Europe
articles.summary: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has called for an end to the war involving Iran as quickly as possible, warning that the conflict is placing a growing economic and security burden...
articles.full_text:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has called for an end to the war involving Iran as quickly as possible, warning that the conflict is placing a growing economic and security burden on Europe, while using his Asian tour to strengthen trade and defense partnerships and address concerns over European protectionism.
Speaking Friday during the final stop of a weeklong visit to Japan, Singapore and South Korea, Merz said the war's consequences for Europe remained severe and that diplomatic efforts to end the fighting were a priority.
The disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global oil and gas supplies, has driven up energy prices and intensified pressure on European economies. Germany, with its energy-intensive industrial sector, has been particularly exposed to the economic fallout.
Merz has repeatedly warned against allowing the conflict to become a prolonged war, arguing that the collapse of the Iranian state or uncontrolled instability across the region would have serious consequences for European security, energy supplies and migration.
While acknowledging concerns over Iran's nuclear and ballistic missile programs and its support for regional armed groups, the German leader has stressed the need for a negotiated settlement that prevents further escalation.
Berlin has been working with European and regional partners, including France, Britain and Gulf states, to support diplomatic efforts and establish conditions for a lasting agreement.
Merz has also linked the restoration of normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz directly to easing pressure on global energy markets, describing the reopening of the waterway as essential to stabilizing fuel and gas prices.
Germany has indicated that it could contribute to securing the strategic waterway after a cease-fire, potentially deploying minehunters and other military assets. However, Merz has made clear that any such involvement would require a cease-fire, an international mandate, preferably from the United Nations, and approval from the Bundestag.
The conflict has also tested relations between Europe and the United States, with European leaders increasingly concerned about the economic costs of a prolonged military campaign.
Merz has maintained that his relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump remains functional despite differences over the war's direction and how it should end.
Against this backdrop, Merz has sought to strengthen Germany's economic relationships across Asia, a region increasingly important to European trade and industrial supply chains.
Speaking Friday at the Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business in Seoul, he pledged to raise concerns expressed by Asian trading partners about the European Union's proposed "Made in Europe" initiatives with officials in Brussels.
The initiatives, intended to strengthen European industrial production and competitiveness, have raised concerns among some trading partners that the bloc could turn toward protectionism and restrict access to its markets.
"There is a fear that we might be facing a new wave of European protectionism, that we are closing ourselves off from other nations," Merz said.
"I take these concerns very seriously. I will carry them back not just to Berlin, but also to Brussels, and I will certainly raise the fact that these concerns were expressed to me quite forcefully here," he added.
Merz said the European Union should take the lead in defending international trade and the rules-based global economic system at a time when free trade faces growing pressure.
"We want to offer opportunities beyond bilateral agreements," he said, adding that Germany was prepared to work with like-minded partners in Europe and elsewhere to protect and further develop the international economic order.
He noted that international trade had contributed significantly to the prosperity of many countries and that governments were reluctant to abandon the benefits of an interconnected global economy.
His remarks came amid concerns over U.S. tariffs and China's state-backed industrial expansion, which have prompted European countries to reconsider their economic dependencies and strengthen domestic industries.
During his Asian tour, Merz sought to deepen Germany's economic and defense relationships with countries facing similar challenges in an increasingly uncertain international environment.
In South Korea, he met President Lee Jae-myung on Thursday, with the two leaders agreeing to establish an enhanced security partnership.
Merz also pointed to similarities between German and South Korean industries, saying they offered opportunities for closer cooperation.
South Korea's Industry Ministry said nine memorandums of understanding had been signed by companies and organizations from the two countries. The agreements cover cooperation in electricity, energy and biohealth, alongside support for startups and efforts to facilitate access to each other's markets.
The South Korean visit followed earlier stops in Japan and Singapore, where Merz also sought to strengthen economic and strategic cooperation.

articles.title: Ex-Biden officials urge 2028 Democrats to reject Gaza policy

A group of former U.S. officials who resigned over the Biden administration's support for Israel's war on Gaza urged Democratic presidential hopefuls Wednesday to condemn Washington's role in the conflict and exclude officials responsible for the policy from future administrations.
Twelve former officials who stepped down between late 2023 and mid-2024 over former President Joe Biden's handling of the Gaza war issued a joint statement calling on candidates seeking the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028 to distance themselves from his administration's policies.
"We call on candidates for the 2028 Presidential Nomination to commit to not hire any administration official directly responsible for enabling Israel's military actions in Gaza," the group said.
The former officials also demanded that prospective candidates acknowledge what they described as Washington's complicity in Israel's genocide in Gaza.
A video accompanying the statement featured images of senior Biden administration figures, including former Secretary of State Antony Blinken and former national security adviser Jake Sullivan, highlighting officials associated with U.S. policy toward Israel during the conflict.
The appeal comes as divisions over U.S. support for Israel continue to shape debate within the Democratic Party ahead of the 2028 presidential race.
Biden's administration faced sustained criticism from progressive lawmakers, activists and human rights advocates over its continued military assistance and diplomatic backing for Israel despite mounting Palestinian civilian casualties and widespread destruction in Gaza.
Prominent progressive Democrats, including U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, have opposed Washington's support for Israeli military operations in Gaza and Lebanon, as well as the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran.
Their criticism has also focused on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's close political ties with Republicans, amid growing divisions within the Democratic Party over relations with Israel.
Several international human rights organizations, legal experts and United Nations investigations have concluded that Israel's military campaign in Gaza constitutes genocide.
Blinken and Sullivan previously voiced concerns over civilian deaths in Gaza, although the Biden administration continued providing military and diplomatic support to Israel throughout the conflict.
The former officials' intervention adds to pressure on prospective Democratic presidential candidates to clarify their positions on U.S. military assistance to Israel and the role of senior Biden-era policymakers in any future administration.

articles.title: Netanyahu uses fake image to exaggerate Arab voter turnout
articles.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been accused of using an AI-generated fake image to exaggerate Arab voter turnout in the Oct. 27 parliamentary elections. Netanyahu on...
articles.full_text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been accused of using an AI-generated fake image to exaggerate Arab voter turnout in the Oct. 27 parliamentary elections.
Netanyahu on Tuesday posted an image X showing people outside a polling station, claiming it depicted Arab voters in the southern city of Rahat.
"This is what is happening today in Rahat. You cannot stay home; go out immediately and vote Likud. We are fighting for our homeland," he wrote.
The British public broadcaster BBC, however, later analyzed the image and identified it as AI-generated or manipulated.
Netanyahu also shared a photograph of Tibi standing in front of a bus, which the Arab lawmaker had posted on his own X account several days earlier.
"Buses are heading toward polling stations, and reports indicate long queues in Arab towns," Netanyahu wrote.
He claimed that right-wing strongholds appeared slow to mobilize, warning his supporters that failing to vote could result in a government led by Arab parties.
The Joint List, an alliance of three Arab parties in Israel, also dismissed and challenged the claims.
In a statement condemning Netanyahu's conduct, the Joint List said the image purportedly showing voters in Rahat was "not real and generated by artificial intelligence."
The alliance accused Netanyahu of using fabricated images to incite against Arabs.
"Netanyahu is afraid of high turnout in our community because he knows it will bring down his government," it said.
The alliance warned that the image presented a misleading picture that could lull Arab voters into staying home by suggesting participation was already sufficiently high.
While turnout in Arab communities was encouraging, it said, a gap remained compared with the wider Israeli electorate, particularly in right-wing strongholds and settlements.
It urged Arab voters to continue heading to polling stations despite obstacles.
Arab lawmaker Ahmad Tibi, meanwhile, said that turnout in Jewish towns remained significantly higher than in Arab communities.
In a video statement Tuesday, he said that Arab participation was being misrepresented by the Israeli right.
"Since the morning, turnout in Arab towns has indeed been higher than in the past, but turnout in Jewish towns is higher, and there is a large gap between turnout in Jewish and Arab communities," he added.
Arab citizens account for 18% of eligible voters while Israeli citizens constitutes 77%, according to figures released by Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics two days earlier.

articles.title: Netanyahu left on shaky ground after losing election majority
articles.summary: Israel's final election results have left Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu without a parliamentary majority, setting the stage for difficult coalition negotiations in which Arab-l...
articles.full_text:
Israel's final election results have left Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu without a parliamentary majority, setting the stage for difficult coalition negotiations in which Arab-led parties could determine who forms the next government.
Results released early Friday showed Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while the main opposition bloc secured 48. Arab-led parties captured the remaining 19 seats, their strongest showing to date, putting them in a potentially decisive position as rival camps seek the 61 seats required to govern.
Neither Netanyahu nor his main challenger, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has an obvious path to a majority. Both must negotiate with parties whose ideological differences and competing demands could make an agreement difficult.
"Now comes the truly hard part," centrist politician Yair Lapid said on X, urging Israelis to remain patient.
The biggest question is whether Eisenkot and other opposition leaders will cooperate with Arab-led parties to remove Netanyahu or abandon their campaign promises and consider joining a government led by the prime minister.
One potential route to an anti-Netanyahu government would involve Eisenkot's bloc joining forces with Arab-led parties, potentially creating a 67-seat majority. Even without formally joining the coalition, the Arab parties could provide the support needed for a minority government.
However, such an arrangement would carry considerable political risks for Eisenkot and his Jewish allies.
Arab citizens make up about 20% of Israel's population. Many are Palestinians whose families remained within the country's borders after the 1948 Nakba.
They maintain close ties with Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza, contributing to longstanding suspicion among many Jewish Israelis.
An Arab party joined an Israeli governing coalition for the first time in 2021, when the United Arab List became part of a government that lasted approximately 18 months.
Netanyahu has portrayed renewed cooperation as a betrayal of Israel's Jewish identity and a national security threat, increasing pressure on right-leaning opposition lawmakers to reject such an alliance.
Hundreds of Israelis have meanwhile demonstrated, urging Eisenkot and his allies to work with Arab-led parties rather than allow Netanyahu to remain in power. Strong Arab turnout also reflected opposition to Netanyahu's far-right allies, particularly National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose party lost seats.
Another possibility would involve Netanyahu persuading Eisenkot or some of his right-leaning allies to abandon their opposition and join a unity government.
Such an arrangement could potentially secure a 67-seat majority but would require significant compromises.
Eisenkot and his allies have repeatedly ruled out serving under Netanyahu, blaming him for the security failures surrounding Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, incursion and accusing him of undermining democratic institutions. They have also cited his ongoing corruption trial as a reason he should leave office.
Joining a Netanyahu-led government would risk alienating voters who supported the opposition to secure a change in leadership. One of their central demands is an official inquiry into the failures preceding Oct. 7.
Netanyahu could also seek to exploit divisions within the opposition by approaching right-wing politicians Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman. Both support settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank but have longstanding disputes with Netanyahu and oppose military exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Jewish men, a major demand of his religious allies.
The negotiations are unfolding amid controversy over unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties manipulated the election, potentially with foreign assistance.
Before the final results were announced, Netanyahu and his Likud party amplified claims that Arab-led parties had stolen the election.
Opposition figures accused the prime minister of undermining the legitimacy of Arab voters and inflaming tensions against a population representing about one-fifth of Israel's citizens.
In his first public response Friday, Netanyahu posted on X that forming a coalition with Arab parties was forbidden.
Noam Sohlberg, head of Israel's election committee and a Supreme Court justice, said serious suspicions of foreign interference had been brought to his attention. Although he could not verify the claims, he requested an investigation by the Shin Bet security agency.
Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu's party had accused Qatar of involvement. The Gulf country rejected the allegations as "ridiculous and dangerous."
The election committee said the investigation was based on classified intelligence but stressed that it would not affect the final results or target any particular section of the population. Acting Director General Dean Livne also warned against unfounded reports surrounding the inquiry.
The Shin Bet said its investigation was not intended to cast suspicion on an entire community that had exercised its democratic right to vote lawfully. The election committee described allegations of systematic electoral violations as baseless and requested the agency's findings within a week.
If neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot secures a majority, Israel could face another election early next year, with Netanyahu's government remaining in a caretaker capacity.
A fresh vote could hurt the opposition, which entered the latest contest with considerable momentum but failed to secure an outright majority. Tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad reportedly travelled home to vote, raising questions about whether they would make the same journey again.
Netanyahu could use the additional time to strengthen his position. Several smaller parties aligned with him failed to cross the electoral threshold required to enter parliament, leaving some pro-Netanyahu votes without representation. Their supporters could shift toward larger right-wing parties in another election.
Israel previously endured five elections in three and a half years following a similar political deadlock in 2019.
Losing office would also expose Netanyahu to increased pressure over his corruption allegations and calls for an official investigation into the security failures surrounding the Oct. 7 incursion.
The results must be certified and submitted to President Isaac Herzog next Wednesday. He will then select a candidate to attempt to form a government. The new Knesset is expected to be sworn in Nov. 10.
Herzog has pledged to do everything possible to prevent another election, but Israel's political future remains uncertain as party leaders prepare for negotiations that could reshape the country's government.

articles.title: US defense chief fires senior general over alleged classified leaks
articles.summary: U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has dismissed Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, a senior military planner serving on the Pentagon's Joint Staff, following allegations that he disclos...
articles.full_text:
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has dismissed Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, a senior military planner serving on the Pentagon's Joint Staff, following allegations that he disclosed classified information to the public, officials said Thursday.
Sylvia's firing is one of the highest-profile consequences to date from Hegseth's sweeping hunt for officials suspected of leaking information to the news media as the unpopular Iran war enters its ninth month.
Hegseth's effort includes a Pentagon task force to identify the source of leaks and the widespread use of polygraph exams on senior officials as part of these investigations.
Last year, he introduced a media policy that raised legal concerns among press organizations, and revoked the press credentials of journalists who refused to sign it.
A senior Pentagon official, speaking on condition of anonymity, accused Sylvia of failing three polygraphs questioning him about leaking classified information.
"The extent of his leaking became so critical that Secretary Hegseth took immediate action and fired Sylvia in order to protect national security. Urgent action was needed and could not wait another second," the official said.
US President Donald Trump, who misidentified Sylvia as a woman, said the senior U.S. general has "got problems."
"We're very much looking for leakers, and she's going to have big problems, long-term problems," Trump told reporters.
Sylvia could not be immediately reached for comment.
Sylvia led the Directorate for Strategy, Plans, and Policy at the Joint Staff, known inside the military as the J5, a key position that helps advise the top U.S. military official, General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
He previously led the U.S. Army's 101st Airborne Division. His dismissal was first reported by The Atlantic magazine.
His removal comes as the U.S. military plans for a potential resumption of intensive bombings in Iran, something Trump has called "another little Epic Fury." The Pentagon has fumed about leaks during the Iran war, including about its planning and the expenditure of munitions.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that an internal U.S. military analysis estimates it would cost more than $29 billion in munitions alone to restock weapons used against Iran so far. That's the bulk of the more than $47 billion spent on operations in the war.
Sean Parnell, the chief Pentagon spokesperson, said the decision followed an extensive investigation by the Air Force Office of Special Investigations.
"This matter, along with others, have been referred to the Justice Department for potential further legal action," Parnell said, without identifying other officials who may also be targeted.
Parnell added: "Our commitment was not an empty promise. We vowed to find you, and we meant it."
A spokesperson for the Joint Staff withdrew an initial statement expressing gratitude for Sylvia's 32 years of service, saying "we determined the statement did not appropriately reflect the full circumstances."
"Out of respect for the service member and the ongoing personnel process, we will not comment further," the spokesperson said.

articles.title: Hegseth's latest Pentagon purge ousts top military planner Sylvia
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired the Pentagon’s top military planner, a defense official said Wednesday, in the latest ouster of a senior military officer as President Donald T...
articles.full_text:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired the Pentagon’s top military planner, a defense official said Wednesday, in the latest ouster of a senior military officer as President Donald Trump weighs renewed strikes on Iran amid an eight-month war.
Hegseth removed Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff. Sylvia is the second general officer Hegseth ousted from the post, known in military circles as the J5. He forced Sylvia's predecessor, Lt. Gen. Joseph McGee, to retire last October.
The defense official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel matters, said no immediate replacement for Sylvia is planned and no reason was given for the firing. The Atlantic earlier reported the move.
A spokesperson for the Joint Staff expressed "deepest gratitude to Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia and his family for their 32 years of distinguished service to our nation" and wished him and his family the best.
Typically, the J5 director and staff are responsible for generating and coordinating military plans with both the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs and the U.S. President. Sylvia's firing comes as U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly proposed new military operations against Iran.
U.S. President Donald Trump has vowed to "finish the job" in Iran after launching the war with Israel eight months ago and said new strikes are an option after next week's midterm elections.
U.S. officials have told several Middle Eastern countries and regional allies to prepare for potential renewed military action after Tuesday's elections, as well as the possibility Iran will retaliate against them, two diplomats briefed on the matter said. They say U.S. President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on new strikes.
A third U.S. aircraft carrier and thousands more troops are heading to the region.
Before arriving at the Joint Staff, Sylvia served as the commander of the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, until May 2025, according to his official biography, now offline. He also previously served as the vice director of the J5.
He is the latest of nearly two dozen general and flag officers and other military leaders Hegseth has removed or forced to retire during his tenure. The Pentagon has not publicly explained almost all of these departures. These include the civilian secretaries of the Army and Navy and some top uniformed officers for the military services.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment late Wednesday.
Hegseth said last month he ordered the military to double cuts to top officers, aiming for a 20% decrease to be completed by Jan. 1, 2027. Approximately 800 flag and general officer positions currently exist.
"I call it accountability and long overdue," Hegseth told junior officers and enlisted leaders at Marine Corps Base Quantico on Sept. 30.
Some members of Congress criticize cuts to general officer ranks as a "purge" that will take years to rebuild.
"He's got some kind of deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military," Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a former Navy combat pilot who criticizes Hegseth, said last month. "He's purging a generation of great military leaders, and it will take a generation to recover from it."

articles.title: 27 Ugandans recruited by Russia killed or presumed dead in Ukraine
articles.summary: Twenty-seven Ugandans recruited into Russia’s military have been killed or are presumed dead while fighting in Ukraine, according to diplomatic correspondence that highlights growi...
articles.full_text:
Twenty-seven Ugandans recruited into Russia’s military have been killed or are presumed dead while fighting in Ukraine, according to diplomatic correspondence that highlights growing concerns over the recruitment of African nationals into Moscow’s war effort.
A letter dated Oct. 17 from Uganda’s embassy in Moscow to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Kampala listed 11 citizens whose deaths had been confirmed and 16 others whose bodies could not be located, including through searches of prisoner-of-war records.
Reuters obtained the letter Thursday, Oct. 29, and an official at Uganda’s foreign ministry confirmed its authenticity.
The document, signed by Uganda’s ambassador to Russia, Moses K. Kizige, said the information had been provided by Russia’s Foreign Ministry through a diplomatic communication known as a note verbale, following an earlier inquiry by the Ugandan embassy.
The embassy had sought information in August about approximately 35 Ugandans believed to be serving in Russia’s so-called special military operation in Ukraine.
Of the 27 men now listed as dead or missing, Russian authorities confirmed the deaths of 11, while the remaining 16 have not been accounted for. Their remains have not been recovered, and their names do not appear on available prisoner-of-war lists.
The embassy effectively considers the missing men dead, although their individual circumstances and the locations where they disappeared remain unclear.
The correspondence also identified five Ugandans who remain under contract with the Russian military. They are expected to leave service when their contracts expire.
Another citizen, Robert Tumwebaze, was reportedly dismissed from military service after receiving treatment at a military hospital in Nizhny Novgorod. He subsequently left embassy personnel at a railway station, according to the letter.
Ambassador Kizige urged Uganda’s foreign ministry to inform the families of the deceased as soon as possible so they could pursue compensation and other benefits potentially available under their relatives' Russian military contracts.
Russia's embassy in Kampala did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The deaths add to mounting concerns across Africa over the recruitment of citizens into Russia's military, with increasing reports of men travelling to the country after being promised civilian employment before finding themselves deployed to the front lines in Ukraine.
Investigations and accounts from relatives have described recruitment offers involving well-paid jobs as drivers, security guards, construction workers and cooks. Some recruits reportedly discovered only after arriving in Russia that they were expected to sign military contracts and participate in combat operations.
In several cases, families have struggled to establish contact with relatives after they travelled to Russia, while others have reported that recruits had their passports and mobile phones confiscated, leaving them with little ability to seek help or return home.
Ukraine has repeatedly raised concerns about the involvement of African nationals in Russia's military campaign. Ukrainian officials said last year that more than 1,400 citizens from approximately three dozen African countries were fighting alongside Russian forces, with some allegedly recruited through deception.
An investigation by Journalists For Justice identified at least 3,034 Africans from 40 countries who had enlisted in Russia's military since October 2022. At least 502 deaths had been documented by the end of June 2026.
Kenya, Ghana and South Africa have been among the countries most vocal about the recruitment of their citizens, with governments raising the issue through diplomatic channels and warning people against accepting suspicious employment offers in Russia.
Kenya has reported hundreds of its citizens becoming involved in the conflict, with dozens killed or missing. Nairobi has also pursued diplomatic engagement with Moscow over the recruitment of Kenyans and efforts to secure the return of those caught up in the war.
The concerns have spread beyond East Africa, with families and authorities in countries including Uganda, Cameroon, Nigeria and Ghana seeking information about citizens believed to have joined Russian forces.
The Ugandan embassy's correspondence does not establish how each of the 27 men was recruited, whether they knowingly signed up for combat service or which battles they may have fought in. However, relatives of some Ugandans involved have previously said their family members travelled to Russia after receiving offers of civilian employment before losing contact with them.
The latest diplomatic disclosures also come amid reports that recruitment networks are increasingly targeting other African countries as governments step up efforts to discourage their citizens from joining Russia's military.
Russia has repeatedly denied illegally recruiting African nationals to fight in Ukraine, maintaining that foreign citizens serving in its armed forces do so voluntarily under formal military contracts.
Moscow has also argued that it has sufficient manpower for its military operations and does not need to resort to coercive recruitment.
However, investigations into recruitment networks have raised questions about the role of intermediaries who allegedly use misleading job advertisements to attract foreign workers before directing them toward military service.
Some investigations and United Nations-related findings have also highlighted possible trafficking and exploitation involving recruitment brokers.

articles.title: Ethiopia clashes drive 50,000 people into Kenya: UN
articles.summary: Nearly 50,000 people have fled southern Ethiopia into neighboring Kenya amid fighting that erupted last week, the United Nations said Wednesday, citing figures provided by local au...
articles.full_text:
Nearly 50,000 people have fled southern Ethiopia into neighboring Kenya amid fighting that erupted last week, the United Nations said Wednesday, citing figures provided by local authorities.
The figure represents a sharp jump from the 36,000 recorded on Tuesday by UNHCR, the U.N. refugee agency, in the wake of clashes between the armies of southern Ethiopia's Somali and Oromia regions.
"According to local authorities, up to an estimated 50,000 people have crossed into Kenya," said Fatima Mohammed-Cole, the UNHCR representative for Kenya.
That number could quickly change given the situation on the ground, with fresh crossings being recorded, Mohammed-Cole warned.
The unrest was sparked on Oct. 20 after a Somali regional flag was hoisted in Moyale, a city jointly administered between Somali and Oromia. Several people have died in clashes, sources told AFP on Saturday.
Many of those who had fled were women and children, Mohammed-Cole said.
"While some are staying with relatives and host communities, others have sought shelter in temporary locations like schools and churches," she added.
UNHCR has sent an emergency team to the region and is working with the Kenyan government, alongside other humanitarian organisations such as the Red Cross, to provide aid to those displaced.
Ethiopia, Africa's second most populous country at some 130 million people, is the scene of various armed conflicts across its vast territory.
The borderlands of its various regions, whose tracing dates back to 1991, are often the source of clashes.
For several years, the federal government has been locked in conflict with rebel movements in the Oromia and Amhara regions, the country's most populous.
After months of tensions, fighting has also broken out again in the northern Tigray region, already the scene of a devastating war from 2020 to 2022.
Diplomatic disagreements with neighbouring Eritrea have likewise led to fears of another conflict between the fractious Horn of Africa neighbors.

articles.title: EU divided over proposed associate membership for Canada: Report
articles.summary: European Union member states have failed to reach consensus on granting Canada "associate membership" status, with at least four countries objecting to the term's inclusion in a jo...
articles.full_text:
European Union member states have failed to reach consensus on granting Canada "associate membership" status, with at least four countries objecting to the term's inclusion in a joint summit statement, Politico reported Tuesday.
EU ambassadors failed to reach an agreement on the wording during talks Monday, according to the report.
A subsequent attempt to approve the statement through a so-called silence procedure also failed after Germany and at least three other countries raised objections before Tuesday's midday deadline, two EU diplomats told Politico.
The issue is expected to return to the agenda at another meeting of EU ambassadors Wednesday, a day before the EU-Canada summit begins in Montreal.
Germany is leading efforts to remove the term "associate membership" entirely from the proposed text, the diplomats said.
The disagreement reflects divisions within the bloc over the proposed status, which European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen suggested to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney during her State of the Union address in Strasbourg last month.
Four EU diplomats previously told Politico that von der Leyen had not consulted member state capitals before putting forward the proposal.
Von der Leyen, European Council President Antonio Costa, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and several European commissioners are expected to travel to Montreal for the Oct. 29-30 summit.
The talks are expected to focus on strengthening EU-Canada relations and expanding cooperation in trade, energy, education and the Arctic.

articles.title: Bolsonaro touches down in US as legal pressure mounts in Brazil
articles.summary: Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro arrived in Miami with his family on Wednesday after refusing to comply with a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports, escalating tensions...
articles.full_text:
Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro arrived in Miami with his family on Wednesday after refusing to comply with a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports, escalating tensions between Brasilia and Washington following his defeat in Sunday's presidential election.
The U.S. government has said it will grant entry visas to Bolsonaro and his family, despite the Brazilian investigation into alleged corruption and money laundering. Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing.
Reuters TV footage showed Bolsonaro, his wife and their two daughters disembarking from a Gulfstream G400 private jet at Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport.
Their journey to the United States unfolded across several countries under a cloud of secrecy. Argentina's migration department said the family entered northern Argentina late Tuesday before traveling by private jet to Guayaquil, Ecuador, and then continuing to Miami.
Argentina's presidency, Ecuadorian government ministries and Baires Fly, the private jet operator, did not respond to requests for comment.
The arrival followed conflicting reports about Bolsonaro's whereabouts. CNN and The Washington Post reported Tuesday that he had reached the United States, citing anonymous sources, while a Brazilian police source told AFP there was no formal record of his departure.
The source also said Bolsonaro's Brazilian and diplomatic passports had been canceled. However, the senator has held Italian nationality since 2023, according to an Italian parliamentary document reviewed by AFP.
Bolsonaro's departure threatens to further strain relations between the two largest countries in the Americas, as Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has accused Washington of helping the Bolsonaro family regain power.
Reuters reported before Sunday's election on a U.S. State Department campaign aimed at restoring the family to office.
U.S. President Donald Trump, a close ally of Bolsonaro's father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, said Wednesday he supported Flavio Bolsonaro coming to the United States. The State Department had announced a day earlier that it would issue visas to the senator and his family.
Trump has repeatedly portrayed Jair Bolsonaro as a victim of political and judicial persecution in Brazil. He also claimed Monday that Brazil's election was rigged following Flavio Bolsonaro's defeat, without providing evidence.
Jair Bolsonaro traveled to the United States in December 2022 after losing that year's presidential election to Lula and refusing to concede. He returned to Brazil three months later and was eventually sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup following his supporters' storming of government buildings in Brasilia.
Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, had campaigned on a pledge to secure his father's release. He was widely expected to win Sunday's election after finishing ahead of Lula in the first round, but the incumbent secured 51.8% of the vote in the final round.
The senator rejected the result and said he would seek to have it annulled, citing an extension of polling hours intended to address transportation difficulties that prevented some voters from reaching polling stations. Both campaigns had requested an extension, with Bolsonaro's team citing bad weather in parts of the country.
Bolsonaro's decision to leave Brazil came days after a Supreme Court justice ordered him to surrender his passports. The senator had said Monday he intended to comply and defend himself against what he described as an attempt to intimidate him.
"I have never thought about leaving the country," he said. "I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me."
His defeat also puts his legal position at greater risk. Bolsonaro is expected to lose parliamentary immunity when his Senate term ends in February, potentially exposing him to further legal action.
His campaign manager, Rogerio Marinho, said Tuesday he had been unable to establish the senator's whereabouts.
Marinho told reporters in Brasilia that Bolsonaro had sent him a text message that morning, saying he would wait before speaking to the campaign team. He said he had received no further communication and expressed shock at reports that the senator had left the country.
Lula condemned the reported departure, calling it shameful and suggesting it raised questions about Bolsonaro's intentions.
Separately, Brazil's Supreme Court on Tuesday ordered police to investigate alleged foreign financing of Bolsonaro's campaign and possible overseas interference, including the manipulation of social media.
Lula's campaign had accused Meta, the parent company of WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, of algorithmic manipulation that affected the election. Meta denied favoring either candidate, although it acknowledged that some of Lula's campaign advertisements had been mistakenly deactivated because of technical errors.
