articles.title: Trump says Putin-Zelenskyy meeting to be arranged 'very soon'
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday that a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy could be arranged soon, as Moscow offer...
articles.full_text:
U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday that a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy could be arranged soon, as Moscow offered to host direct talks in the Russian capital and diplomatic efforts intensified to end the war.
Trump expressed optimism about progress in negotiations but gave no date or location for a potential summit. His remarks came as Russian officials discussed resuming trilateral talks with Ukraine and the United States in Abu Dhabi, while European leaders stepped up contacts with Moscow and Kyiv.
“I think with Russia, we’re making a lot of progress with Russia-Ukraine. There’ll be a meeting set up here soon,” Trump told reporters after returning from Texas, where he had attended midterm election campaign rallies.
Asked about the timing, Trump said the meeting would happen “over the next not too long.” He added that progress could be achieved without a face-to-face meeting between the two leaders.
The comments offered no confirmation that Putin and Zelenskyy had agreed to meet. Neither Kyiv nor Moscow had publicly confirmed an arrangement for a leaders' summit following Trump's remarks.
The latest diplomatic push comes as the war, launched by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, continues to exact a heavy human and economic toll. Trump's administration has pursued negotiations since he returned to the White House in January 2025, but efforts to secure a settlement have yet to produce a breakthrough.
Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said Tuesday that Putin had invited Zelenskyy to Moscow for direct negotiations, promising that security arrangements would be made for the Ukrainian leader.
According to Russia's state-run TASS news agency, Ushakov said Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb had informed Putin during a recent telephone conversation that Zelenskyy was interested in meeting him directly.
“Our boss reiterated that if Zelenskyy truly wishes to hold direct negotiations, he should come to Moscow, where all necessary conditions, including those regarding his safety, will be provided for him,” Ushakov said, according to TASS.
The invitation leaves a major question unresolved: whether Zelenskyy would accept Moscow as the venue for negotiations with a leader whose forces continue to occupy Ukrainian territory.
Zelenskyy has repeatedly called for direct talks with Putin, arguing that territorial disputes and other fundamental questions about the war's future require decisions at the highest level. He has also insisted that Ukraine must participate in any negotiations affecting its sovereignty and future security.
There was no immediate indication that Kyiv had accepted the Moscow invitation.
Ushakov said the recent 90-minute telephone conversation between Putin, Stubb and Støre focused largely on plans to resume negotiations involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States.
The discussions could take place in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, in the first half of November, although a final date and venue had not been confirmed.
“There were many questions on this matter and requests for clarification from our side,” Ushakov said, describing the call as thorough and substantive.
He added that the parties had agreed to speak again if necessary.
Ushakov also said the question of European representation in future negotiations had not yet been addressed, suggesting that Moscow was not currently considering who might represent the continent at the negotiating table.
The position highlights a potential point of friction between Russia and European governments, which have sought a role in shaping any settlement because of its implications for European security.
The latest diplomatic activity follows meetings between U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Ukrainian and European officials in Oslo on Oct. 20, followed by discussions with Putin in St. Petersburg the next day.
Those contacts covered possible peace arrangements, security guarantees and postwar economic issues.
Russian officials subsequently indicated that Moscow was prepared in principle to resume technical-level negotiations with Ukraine and the United States.
Zelenskyy has supported restarting the talks, while arguing that working groups should address technical matters and prepare the ground for a meeting between the leaders.
He has also maintained that any agreement affecting Ukraine must involve Kyiv directly.
Despite renewed diplomatic activity, the prospects for a breakthrough remain uncertain because Moscow and Kyiv continue to disagree over the fundamental terms of a settlement.
Putin has demanded Russian control over occupied Ukrainian territories, including areas Moscow claims but does not fully control. Russia has also opposed a broad cease-fire before an agreement on the main terms of a settlement, arguing that a pause in fighting could allow Ukraine to strengthen its military.
Ukraine has rejected demands to surrender territory and insists that any peace agreement must protect its sovereignty and provide credible security guarantees against another Russian invasion.
Zelenskyy has argued that territorial disputes cannot be resolved by treating occupied land as a matter of geography alone, pointing to the lives lost defending Ukrainian communities.
The Ukrainian president has also warned against easing sanctions on Russia before meaningful progress is made, arguing that doing so would weaken Kyiv's negotiating position.
Relations between Trump and Zelenskyy have been strained by disagreements over the pace and terms of negotiations. Trump has pressed Ukraine to reach a settlement, while Zelenskyy has resisted proposals that could compromise the country's territorial integrity or leave it vulnerable to renewed Russian aggression.
The prospect of a meeting in Moscow could prove particularly difficult given the ongoing war and the two governments' competing demands. Although Ushakov said Russia would guarantee Zelenskyy's safety, no agreement on a venue has been announced.
The renewed push for negotiations comes as fighting and attacks continue across Ukraine, with both countries facing mounting military and economic costs.
Trump's administration has pursued several diplomatic channels, while European leaders have sought to ensure that any settlement accounts for the security of Ukraine and its neighbors.
A separate, limited cease-fire around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson region has also offered a narrow opening for humanitarian cooperation. The arrangement, reached with the involvement of U.S. First Lady Melania Trump, is intended to facilitate aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
However, local humanitarian arrangements have yet to translate into a broader halt to hostilities.
Trump's latest remarks signal Washington's continued effort to bring the Russian and Ukrainian leaders into direct negotiations. But his prediction that a meeting will take place “very soon” remains an expectation rather than a confirmed diplomatic agreement.

articles.title: 'Nobody heard us': Gen Z ups ante as protests sweep across Europe
articles.summary: A wave of youth-led protests is sweeping across Europe, with Generation Z demanding better education, affordable housing, economic opportunities and action against corruption, as g...
articles.full_text:
A wave of youth-led protests is sweeping across Europe, with Generation Z demanding better education, affordable housing, economic opportunities and action against corruption, as growing frustration with political leaders fuels demonstrations from France to Serbia and Albania.
In Brussels, 19-year-old student Maya Gourdel writes a slogan that has become a rallying cry for young people challenging those in power: “If we burn, you burn with us!”
Borrowed from the 2012 film “The Hunger Games,” the phrase has been adopted by youth movements worldwide, reflecting the anger of a generation that feels excluded from decisions shaping its future.
From the suburbs of Paris to the streets of Belgrade, thousands of young people have protested deteriorating school facilities, limited job prospects, rising living costs, corruption and a lack of political accountability.
Some demonstrations have turned violent, with thousands of shops damaged or looted in France in recent weeks and police deploying stun grenades and water cannons.
But the protests have also delivered a major political breakthrough. In Serbia, nearly two years of student-led demonstrations against perceived corruption and growing authoritarianism culminated in the electoral defeat of longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic this weekend.
“Waking up, the first thing we felt was certainly a sense of relief and freedom,” said Stasa Piletic, a student protester. “Personally, I feel a sense of victory. I feel that we finally moved from protests to responsibility.”
For many young Europeans, the protests reflect a growing belief that traditional political institutions have failed to address their concerns.
Chiara, a 21-year-old student in Milan, said spontaneous demonstrations had created an opportunity for collective action after years of mounting frustration.
“I think the worst damage this ruling class has done to my generation is stealing even the ability to imagine a future, to dream,” she said.
Italian students face schools struggling with teacher shortages and deteriorating buildings, followed by the prospect of poorly paid jobs and increasingly unaffordable housing, she said.
The unrest reflects a broader international trend. Generation Z, generally defined as people born between 1997 and 2012, has mobilized against political and economic grievances in countries including Bangladesh in 2024, Nepal in 2025 and India this year.
Europe has now become a focal point.
Rising prices and the cost of living concern 40% of Europeans aged 16 to 30, according to an EU survey published in 2025.
Of the 92.7 million people in the European Union who faced the risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2025, young adults aged 18 to 24 recorded the highest risk, at 26.3%. The rate among people 65 and older was 18.8%.
Young protesters are also questioning how governments distribute resources between younger and older generations.
In France, people over 60 account for about a quarter of the population but own 60% of the country's wealth, according to the OFCE economic research institute.
Public pensions are France's largest category of government spending and are projected to reach 14% of economic output as the population ages. Efforts to raise the retirement age or reduce benefits have faced strong opposition.
France spends less on pensions than Greece and Italy, which devote about 16% of gross domestic product to public pensions, according to 2025 figures from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. Australia, Chile, Iceland, Ireland and South Korea each spend less than 4% of GDP.
A French government report published in October found that pension spending increased by 2.5 percentage points of GDP between 2000 and 2023, while education spending declined by 0.5 percentage points. Pensions also accounted for 32% of the Education Ministry's budget, limiting resources available for other priorities.
For students facing deteriorating classrooms and staff shortages, the figures reinforce concerns that their needs are being overlooked.
In a suburb north of Paris, 17-year-old high school student Bilal Narjissi has protested what he described as deplorable school conditions and staff shortages.
“There used to be rats,” he said.
Students were evacuated last year after a roof collapsed in the school courtyard, although nobody was injured, he said.
Narjissi said the demonstrations had shown that young people across Europe shared common concerns.
“We all agree on one point: that young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren't listened to enough,” he said.
Gourdel, who has also protested for better school conditions in Belgium, said students initially tried peaceful action but struggled to attract attention.
“We tried to do it passively. Nobody heard us. It's only when people started to burn trash or that kind of stuff that the media and cameras started showing us,” she said.
Protests are continuing to spread, with a demonstration planned in Germany this weekend over the cost of living, inequality, war and school conditions.
Albania has also experienced unrest, with student-led demonstrations against Prime Minister Edi Rama's government spreading from Tirana to other cities.
Protesters have voiced anger over perceived corruption, limited employment opportunities and poor education standards.
“Our Prime Minister spent 130 days not listening to us,” said Xyke Kurti, a 19-year-old architecture student.
Kurti said many young Albanians saw emigration as their best chance of securing a future.
“If you ask a student in Albania, 'where do you see your future?' Everyone says 'outside this country',” she said.
She argued that qualifications and talent were often insufficient to guarantee success in a system where personal connections could determine who advances.
Serbia's student movement has achieved what demonstrators elsewhere in Europe are still seeking: an electoral victory after sustained public pressure against an established political leader.
The challenge now is turning protest into effective government. The students and candidates they support have little governing experience, raising questions about their ability to deliver reforms.
Luka Stojakovic, another Serbian protester, dismissed concerns about their inexperience.
“We have seen where people with political experience have brought us,” he said.

articles.title: At least 68 killed as 2 high-speed trains collide in central Spain
articles.summary: At least 68 people were killed Wednesday when a high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train in central Spain, derailing two carriages and leaving wreckage scattered acr...
articles.full_text:
At least 68 people were killed Wednesday when a high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train in central Spain, derailing two carriages and leaving wreckage scattered across a field as emergency crews raced to rescue survivors.
The collision occurred shortly after 9:00 a.m. in Toledo province, on the high-speed rail line connecting Madrid with Seville in southwestern Spain, according to the country's rail infrastructure operator ADIF. Rail services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia were suspended following the crash.
Officials warned that the number of fatalities could rise as rescue workers reached passengers trapped in the wreckage.
Esther Padilla, a spokeswoman for the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, said two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers were traveling in the same direction when one struck the rear of the other, which had stopped. The impact knocked two carriages off the tracks.
The cause of the collision was not immediately known.
The crash occurred on a relatively flat stretch of railway between the towns of Urda and Los Yebenes, surrounded by open fields. Images from the scene showed a carriage severely mangled, with twisted metal and other debris scattered down a gravel slope.
Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia told state broadcaster TVE that emergency crews were concentrating on recovering survivors and bodies from the two most heavily damaged carriages. Injured passengers were being transported to hospitals across the region.
"It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy," García said.
The collision involved a train operated by state-owned Renfe and another run by private company Iryo, which is owned by Italian rail operator Trenitalia. Spanish media reported that the Renfe train struck the stationary Iryo service.
Regional authorities said 397 passengers were aboard the Renfe train and 147 were traveling on the Iryo service, bringing the total number of passengers on the two trains to 544.
Iryo said it had activated its safety protocols and was working closely with authorities following the crash.
Emergency responders, including firefighters, police and civil protection teams, were deployed to the scene. A military emergency brigade was also sent to support rescue operations.
Manuel Galan, mayor of nearby Urda, told TVE that civil protection officials had asked the town council to prepare a sports pavilion to receive injured passengers and others affected by the collision.
Emiliano García-Page, president of Castilla-La Mancha, said on X that he was traveling to the crash site as emergency operations continued.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez canceled his scheduled engagements to focus on the disaster, expressing condolences to the victims and their families.
"I am dismayed by the serious train accident in Toledo," Sánchez wrote on X. "Emergency services are working on site to attend to the affected passengers."
Spain's King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia also expressed their sorrow and said they were following developments.
"We share in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt support to the injured and all those affected," the royal couple said in a statement posted on X.
The disaster is the second major train accident in Spain this year, renewing concerns about safety on a railway network that has become one of the most extensive high-speed systems in the world.
In January, 45 people were killed in southern Spain when a train derailed near Adamuz in Cordoba province and collided with an oncoming train. The disaster was the country's deadliest rail accident since July 2013, when a train derailed near Santiago de Compostela, killing 80 people.
The January crash shook public confidence in Spain's rail network and prompted renewed scrutiny of railway safety. Investigators examining Wednesday's collision will seek to establish how the two trains came to collide and whether any technical or operational failures contributed to the disaster.
Spain has invested heavily in high-speed rail over the past three decades, building a network that connects major cities and serves a population of about 49 million. The country's rail union defines high-speed lines as those designed for trains traveling at 250 kph (155 mph) or faster.
Spain has developed about 3,900 kilometers (2,400 miles) of high-speed track, making it the world's second-largest network after China's, which extends roughly 45,000 kilometers (28,000 miles), according to the International Union of Railways.
The network was opened to private operators only in recent years as Spain sought to introduce competition alongside Renfe. Iryo began operating passenger services in the country in 2022.

articles.title: Ebola outbreak tops 10,000 cases as deaths near 4,900 in DRC
articles.summary: Africa’s latest Ebola outbreak has infected more than 10,000 people, with nearly 4,900 deaths reported in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Congolese health authorities said...
articles.full_text:
Africa’s latest Ebola outbreak has infected more than 10,000 people, with nearly 4,900 deaths reported in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Congolese health authorities said Tuesday.
According to figures from the DRC, 10,060 people have contracted the virus and 4,887 have died since the outbreak was detected in May. It is the country’s largest and deadliest Ebola epidemic.
Cases have also been reported in Kenya and Nigeria, while Uganda, which recorded cases earlier in the outbreak, was declared Ebola-free by the World Health Organization (WHO) in August. The WHO has warned that containing the outbreak across several countries presents a complex challenge.
In the DRC, 2,684 people have recovered from the disease, according to the country’s National Institute of Public Health. The reported figures put the outbreak’s fatality rate at nearly 50%.
One of the main challenges facing the response is the lack of an approved vaccine or specific treatment for the Bundibugyo virus, the strain responsible for the outbreak. Researchers have begun testing whether the Ervebo vaccine, which is effective against the more common Zaire strain, could also protect against Bundibugyo.
After spreading undetected for weeks, the virus was first identified in the northeastern Congolese province of Ituri, marking the DRC’s 17th Ebola outbreak.
It has since spread across parts of the country’s north and east, where violence by armed groups and limited trust in state institutions complicate efforts to contain the disease.
Ituri and North Kivu province account for most reported cases. Parts of North Kivu are controlled by the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group.
After reporting 20 cases and two deaths, Uganda was declared Ebola-free by the WHO in late August.
Kenya, which had not reported a confirmed case until Oct. 6, has recorded nine cases and two deaths. The cases have been linked to a traveler who arrived from the DRC via Uganda.
Nigeria confirmed one case on Oct. 20 involving a 42-year-old Swiss woman who had traveled to Uganda with her husband. She was subsequently evacuated to a hospital in Geneva, Switzerland. Authorities are investigating how she contracted the virus, as she had no known travel history to the DRC.
Jean Kaseya, director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, told Agence France-Presse that the organization was investigating the source of the infection.
“We saw that the genomic sequencing of the Kenyan case is similar to the Nigerian case. And we discovered that yesterday with some cases in Beni,” he said.
“Today it’s an outbreak in three regions. We didn’t see that since we started to have experience of Ebola outbreaks. We were not thinking that Nigeria could be an at risk country.”
When the outbreak was declared, only three health zones in one province were affected, Kaseya said.
“Today we are talking about eight provinces, more than 66 health zones. To give you an idea, it’s like twice the size of the UK.”
Nigerian health authorities had identified 53 contacts of the Swiss woman as they sought to prevent further transmission.
Some experts have raised concerns that the virus could have spread after the couple arrived in Nigeria on Oct. 3.
The WHO said the woman developed symptoms on Oct. 7, sought medical care in Abuja on Oct. 11 and tested positive for the Bundibugyo virus on Oct. 20.
Ugandan officials have rejected suggestions that she contracted the disease while in Uganda.
Efforts to contain the outbreak in the DRC have been hampered by mistrust among some communities.
A nurse was killed and another health worker seriously wounded in the northeastern province of Tshopo on Saturday, according to the WHO.
Marcel Likolo, chief medical officer of the Bafwasende health district, told AFP that young people in the area accused the two workers of trying to infect residents with tablets before attacking them.
The Ebola treatment center where the attack occurred has since closed, Likolo said.
Since Ebola was first identified in 1976, the disease has killed more than 15,000 people across Africa.
Researchers are testing whether the Ervebo vaccine, which has demonstrated effectiveness against the Zaire strain of Ebola, could also provide protection against the Bundibugyo virus.

articles.title: Sudan market drone strike kills at least 36 as Darfur crisis deepens
articles.summary: At least 36 people have been killed in a drone strike on a crowded market in Sudan’s Darfur region, a medical aid organization said Tuesday, as attacks on civilian areas intensify...
articles.full_text:
At least 36 people have been killed in a drone strike on a crowded market in Sudan’s Darfur region, a medical aid organization said Tuesday, as attacks on civilian areas intensify and the country’s humanitarian crisis deepens.
Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF, said Sudanese armed forces struck a market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur, on Monday evening, causing what it described as “complete devastation.” A second drone strike hit a residential area.
The MSF-supported Nyala Teaching Hospital had received 36 bodies by Tuesday, including 21 people dressed in civilian clothing, the organization said. More than 150 injured people had also been treated in the hospital’s emergency department, many suffering from shrapnel wounds and severe burns. Children were among the wounded.
The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been fighting Sudan’s military since April 2023, gave a substantially higher toll, saying 188 civilians had been killed and another 356 injured. The figures could not immediately be independently verified.
The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) had not commented on the attack as of Tuesday.
MSF called on both sides to protect civilians and refrain from attacking markets, residential buildings and essential civilian infrastructure.
The strike is the latest in a series of deadly attacks on civilian gathering places. At least four people were killed and many others injured in a similar drone strike on another market in Nyala on Oct. 16. A separate attack on a market in the Abyei region, near the border with South Sudan, killed at least 80 people.
The United Nations has also reported drone strikes at several locations in the capital, Khartoum, in recent days, including an area near the airport. Other attacks have been reported in West Darfur, South Darfur and North Kordofan.
Drones have become an increasingly prominent feature of Sudan’s civil war. According to the U.N. Human Rights Office, drone strikes killed at least 1,120 civilians during the first half of 2026. Both sides have been accused of carrying out attacks that have endangered civilian lives.
The conflict, which erupted in April 2023, has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced more than 14 million, creating one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
The latest violence comes as Sudan’s government seeks international accountability for atrocities in Darfur, where the RSF’s takeover of El Fasher has left civilians facing severe food shortages, displacement and widespread reports of abuses.
Sudan’s Ambassador to Türkiye, Nadir Yousif Eltayeb, said Tuesday that the international community had failed to take an impartial approach to the conflict and had not done enough to address the suffering of civilians.
Speaking at a meeting on Sudan at the Foundation for Political, Economic and Social Research (SETA) in Ankara, Eltayeb said El Fasher had endured a complete siege for about 30 months, leaving residents dependent on limited aid deliveries.
“About 1 million people were surviving on aid delivered by the armed forces by air. People could not access enough food, to the point that they had to eat tree bark,” he said.
Eltayeb said Sudanese government forces had made more than 200 attempts to break the siege but had failed to restore access to the city.
“The international community has taken a biased approach to this issue, preventing it from being resolved,” he said.
The RSF captured El Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, on Oct. 26, 2025, after about 18 months of fighting and a siege that began in May 2024. The city had been the last major urban center in Darfur under the Sudanese army’s control.
Eltayeb accused foreign countries of supporting the RSF, arguing that the paramilitary group would not have been able to advance without outside assistance. He also alleged that armed groups had deliberately targeted particular tribes in El Fasher.
“What happened in El Fasher is genocide,” he said.
He added that the full death toll in El Fasher and the wider Darfur region remained unknown.
Eltayeb further alleged that pressure from the United Arab Emirates had prevented Sudan from submitting reports on the killings to the U.N. Security Council. He accused Abu Dhabi of supporting armed groups involved in the conflict but acknowledged that the allegations had not been proven.
The UAE has repeatedly denied accusations that it supports the RSF.
“We are seeking justice for Sudan,” Eltayeb said, thanking Türkiye for its support.
The fall of El Fasher marked a major shift in the conflict, but the fighting and its aftermath have left the city’s remaining population facing dire conditions.
The U.N. Human Rights Office said more than 6,000 people were killed during the first three days of attacks after the RSF seized the city. Subsequent reports described killings, forced displacement, torture and sexual violence against civilians.
The U.N. has warned that abuses against civilians, including women and children, have continued, citing reports of executions and sexual violence.
The takeover also triggered a mass exodus. About 138,200 people were displaced from El Fasher and surrounding settlements between Oct. 26, 2025, and March 1, 2026, according to figures provided in the humanitarian assessment.
Before the war, El Fasher had a population of more than 1 million. Its population is now estimated to have fallen below 70,000.
Those who remain face continuing insecurity and severely restricted access to food, medical care and other essential services. The departure of tens of thousands of residents has further strained already limited humanitarian operations across Darfur.

articles.title: Trump strikes warmer tone on Canada despite tariff tensions
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump offered an unusually positive assessment of Canada on Thursday, telling supporters at a rally that Ottawa had been treating Washington "extremely nicely...
articles.full_text:
U.S. President Donald Trump offered an unusually positive assessment of Canada on Thursday, telling supporters at a rally that Ottawa had been treating Washington "extremely nicely" in recent weeks despite ongoing trade tensions fueled by his tariff policies.
Trump, at a campaign rally in Rock Hill, South Carolina, for Republican Senate candidate Darline Graham, said the tariffs he imposed on Canada have had the effect of improving relations.
"They're treating us extremely nicely lately," Trump said.
The U.S. accounted for 71.7% of Canada's merchandise exports in 2025. Prime Minister Mark Carney wants to double exports to other countries over the next decade.
Trump has suggested Canada's proposed EU arrangement could be a "hostile act" and threatened tariffs on Europe if he considered it unfriendly. Asked Wednesday about possible retaliation, a senior Canadian government official told reporters the closer relationship was not directed against the United States but reflected longstanding shared interests.

articles.title: 4 killed, 11 injured as helicopter with EU force crashes in Bosnia
articles.summary: Several people died and many others were injured after a helicopter with the European Union peacekeeping force in Bosnia crashed Thursday in the country's north. A hospital spokesp...
articles.full_text:
Several people died and many others were injured after a helicopter with the European Union peacekeeping force in Bosnia crashed Thursday in the country's north.
A hospital spokesperson said four crew members were killed and 11 injured in the crash of the Italian CH-47 Chinook in an area around the town of Brcko.
The helicopter was on a "routine mission" in the region about 180 kilometers (110 miles) northeast of the capital Sarajevo, the EU force, or EUFOR, said.
It said an investigation was underway and more information would follow later.
Media images showed the wreckage of the helicopter on a flat grassy terrain at Gorica, near Brcko.
The spokesperson for Brcko hospital said three people among the 15 on the helicopter were killed in the crash and a fourth died in hospital.
"Twelve people were brought to our hospital. Unfortunately, a fourth person died from his injuries in hospital," said the spokesperson, Salih Ibrahimbegovic.
The Brcko district mayor, Sinisa Milic, earlier told the Bosnian Serb RTRS television that three people died and 12 received medical care, including one person in critical condition.
EUFOR said earlier in a separate statement that "no civilian infrastructure, property, or vehicles were damaged, and there were no injuries to civilians."
EUFOR's 1,200-soldier mission took over from NATO in 2004 to help maintain security and oversee the military provisions of a peace agreement that ended the 1992-95 war. It operates under a U.N. Security Council mandate.
The current force has several hundred troops from 24 European states, according to its website.

articles.summary: A Greek container ship sank off Bulgaria's coast after being struck by naval drones Wednesday, the Bulgarian government said, as a string of attacks in the western Black Sea fueled...
articles.full_text:
A Greek container ship sank off Bulgaria's coast after being struck by naval drones Wednesday, the Bulgarian government said, as a string of attacks in the western Black Sea fueled growing concerns over the potential spread of the Russia-Ukraine war.
The Liberian-flagged CONTSHIP JET, loaded with 421 containers, was badly damaged by three sea drones as it passed through Bulgaria's Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) - but outside its territorial waters - en route from Haifa in Israel to Constanța in Romania.
The crew of 14 Filipinos and four Ukrainians were all rescued and transferred safely to the Bulgarian port of Varna, Contships Management said.
Video footage verified by Reuters showed a sea drone driving alongside the vessel before turning toward its hull. In a separate video, an explosion was seen, causing the ship to eventually list.
It was not immediately clear who had carried out the attack, which added to growing concerns about the impact of Russia's war in Ukraine on commercial shipping in the area.
Ambrey, a global maritime risk management firm, has analysed footage, reportedly filmed on a handheld device by a crew member on board, showing a matte black, 5-6 meter-long unmanned surface vehicle (USV) approaching the vessel at high speed.
The USV was likely a variant of a Russian drone, said Tomas Alexa, a senior analyst at Ambrey Analytics, adding that its manoeuvres indicated it was controlled remotely.
"Ambrey assessed that the USV was likely a variant of, or derived from, the Russian Murena-300S design," he told Reuters.
At least six ships have been attacked by drones off Bulgaria this month, and about two dozen seafarers are feared dead, according to government statements. While it is not clear who has carried out the attacks, Bulgaria's Prime Minister, Rumen Radev, has said that some of them appear to benefit Russia.
Moscow has denied involvement in recent attacks and did not immediately comment on Wednesday's incident.
Andriy Ryzhenko, a former senior Ukrainian navy officer, said the drone visible in the video does not look similar to any model of Ukrainian naval drone that he is aware of.
Bulgaria, a member of the European Union and NATO, has sought assistance to bolster security off its Black Sea coast.
Bulgarian naval commander Kiril Mihaylov told national television authorities had been alerted to a possible drone attack by a French patrol aircraft, but had been unable to prevent it.
The government said that initial inspections on Thursday had found no visible traces of pollution from the ship, whose cargo included lithium-ion batteries, corrosive liquids and acids and industrial components.

articles.title: Bangladesh worries for water as Ganges treaty with India nears end
articles.summary: Bangladesh fears that failure to renew a 30-year Ganges water-sharing treaty with India before it expires in December could deepen water shortages, threatening tens of millions of...
articles.full_text:
Bangladesh fears that failure to renew a 30-year Ganges water-sharing treaty with India before it expires in December could deepen water shortages, threatening tens of millions of livelihoods.
In Bangladesh's parched Barind region, 72-year-old Bikash Soren remembers when the Ganges River flowing in from neighboring India carried large boats past his village year-round.
"For almost three months a year, you hardly see the river flowing," the Protestant priest said.
Two farmers killed themselves last season, he added, after dwindling water levels devastated their rice and wheat crops.
Shrinking flows in the Ganges have also slashed fish catches in the river, known in Bangladesh as the Padma.
"Where will we find fish now?" said Abu Bakar Siddique, 55, who has switched to fish farming in ponds.
"I used to catch many kinds."
The 2,525-kilometer (1,569-mile) Ganges flows through the world's most populous river basin, home to 655 million people, including more than 50 million in Bangladesh, according to the World Bank.
The 1996 treaty, which expires on Dec. 12, governs dry-season water sharing at India's Farakka Barrage, 20 kilometers upstream of Bangladesh.
But Bangladesh needs a new deal based on "mutual benefit and respect," Rashed al Mahmud Titumir, a prime ministerial adviser who heads a technical committee on water sharing, told AFP.
Disputes over water from 54 cross-border rivers between India and Bangladesh stretch back decades and the Ganges is among the most important.
Malik Fida A. Khan, a former Bangladeshi member of the Joint Rivers Commission, the body overseeing water sharing, said India had built "additional dams" upstream.
"This time, the agreement must include provisions on climate change – and take the entire river basin into account," he said.
Bangladesh said India had not responded to its request to negotiate a treaty renewal.
New Delhi's Foreign Ministry said that "discussions regarding river-related matters" are a matter for the Joint Rivers Commission, which held its last technical talks in May.
The last officially confirmed ministerial-level commission meeting was in 2022 – after a 12-year gap.
And a proposed water-sharing deal for the cross-border Teesta River has been stalled since 2011.
Relations between New Delhi and Dhaka have soured since Bangladesh's former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina fled to old ally India, where she remains, following a 2024 uprising.
Hasina, sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against humanity, has vowed to return to Bangladesh from India in December, the month the treaty she signed expires.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman may also visit India before the treaty expires, according to reports, but no visit has been confirmed.
Disputes date back to 1975, when India opened the 2.2-kilometer-long Farakka Barrage. Bangladesh accused India of diverting most of the water.
The United Nations intervened in the dispute and the countries reached a deal in 1977.
But water-sharing arrangements lapsed a decade later, bringing severe consequences, said Sheikh Rokon of Dhaka-based environmental group Riverine People.
"The Ganges suffered during the years without a treaty, and at least three rivers almost dried up," Rokon said.
One was the Gorai, which carries freshwater into the Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest and a World Heritage site, helping limit saltwater intrusion as sea levels rise.
Bangladesh's largest irrigation project, the Ganges-Kobadak Irrigation Project, designed to water 955 square kilometers of farmland, "became inoperative because of water scarcity," Rokon said.
In May, Dhaka approved the Padma Barrage, a $2.8 billion project intended to ease shortages and include a 113-megawatt hydropower plant.
The 1996 treaty has no automatic extension clause.
"If we fail to reach a deal, I fear the situation will be worse than what we experienced during the years without a treaty," Rokon added.
"Demand for freshwater on both sides has increased significantly."
Even with the treaty in place, the Ganges-Kobadak project has shrunk to 550 square kilometers, according to Bangladeshi state news agency BSS.
"If the river does not carry enough water, the consequences could be disastrous," said Chowdhury Sarwar Jahan, a geology professor at Bangladesh's University of Rajshahi.
Bangladesh's agriculture-dependent economy is already reeling from climate change, which compounds changes in river flows, bringing alternating dry-season shortages and intense monsoon floods that wash away farmland and villages.
In Chapainawabganj district, the river has widened by 3 kilometers in recent years – nearly doubling its size – according to Bangladesh's Water Development Board.
Rehana Khatun, 50, described the "howling sound" as floods destroyed her home in Fielder Bazar village.
"The river turned wild and started swallowing everything along the bank," said Khatun, who now lives in a bamboo shelter.
"And the trauma stays with children long after the waters recede."

articles.title: EU, Canada explore unprecedented associate membership deal
articles.summary: The European ​Union and Canada aim to deepen cooperation on AI, climate, energy and security ⁠as they explore the ⁠possibility of Canada becoming the union's first "associate membe...
articles.full_text:
The European Union and Canada aim to deepen cooperation on AI, climate, energy and security as they explore the possibility of Canada becoming the union's first "associate member," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Thursday.
The term, which many EU countries oppose, has no legal meaning.
Deeper ties to Europe are part of Prime Minister Mark Carney's strategy to reduce Canada's economic and security reliance on the US since President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on Canadian goods. Still, Canada's efforts to draw closer to the EU risk angering Trump as trade talks between Canada and the U.S. continue.
"Our idea is simple: it is an association without accession," von der Leyen said in a speech in Montreal at a Canada-EU summit. "We can build a partnership that comes closer to membership than anything we have done before."
"We can work on everything, from AI and climate to energy or security," she said.
Canadian and EU leaders, however, dropped the idea of associate EU membership from their joint declaration, seen by Reuters, agreeing instead to an "ever closer association."
The declaration, which officials plan to make public on Friday, said work to define the Canada-EU relationship would continue until another summit next year.
Von der Leyen first floated the idea of associate membership for Canada six weeks ago, prompting a rebuke from countries led by Germany that argued they could not agree to a concept that had no legal status and had not been fleshed out, diplomats said.

articles.title: Taiwan claims Pakistan briefly shut airspace to Taiwanese flights
articles.summary: Taiwan on Thursday accused Pakistan of briefly closing its airspace to Taiwanese cargo and passenger flights, while pointing fingers at China of being behind the move. "We suspect...
articles.full_text:
Taiwan on Thursday accused Pakistan of briefly closing its airspace to Taiwanese cargo and passenger flights, while pointing fingers at China of being behind the move.
"We suspect definitely China was behind this," Chen Ming-chi, a top official, said after confirming that Pakistan had closed and reopened its airspace to Taiwanese airlines.
China Airlines and EVA Air, which are both based in Taiwan, normally fly over Pakistan on their Asia-Europe route.
Last weekend, however, they began rerouting their Europe-bound flights further south over the Gulf or further north over Russia, AFP analysis of flight tracking data shows.
Some Taiwanese flights have resumed flying over Pakistan, according to the latest data.
"China Airlines and EVA received a notice from the Pakistan authorities that they will lift the ban, but only temporarily ... till the end of the winter," Chen said.
Neither airline would confirm that Pakistan had closed or reopened its airspace when contacted by AFP.
"We condemn Pakistan, and if China is behind this, I think that is a very bad practice to use its leverage over the countries in the Global South to do that," Chen said.
"I think that gets in the way of the safety of the passengers and the smooth operation of the global supply chain."
Pakistan's Defense Minister Khawaja Asif told Bloomberg News Wednesday that the airspace was closed in adherence with Beijing's "One China policy."
China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters Thursday that "as far as we are aware, there are no obstacles for residents of the Taiwan region to travel internationally."
China claims Taiwan as part of its territory and opposes the self-governed island's participation in international organizations and exchanges with other countries.
Chen said it was the first time a country had closed its airspace to Taiwanese commercial flights.
In April, the Seychelles, Mauritius and Madagascar revoked overflight permits for Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te's flight to Eswatini, Taipei's only African ally, forcing him to postpone the trip.
At the time, Taiwan blamed "intense pressure" from China for the revocation.
"China now learned that this could be an effective way to block our airspace access and therefore sort of further isolate Taiwan," Chen said.
"We see this is the discovery that they can weaponize the airspace assets."
Taiwan does not have formal diplomatic ties with Pakistan, which has close relations with China.
Chen said "many like-minded" countries had assisted Taiwan over the airspace closure.
"We are afraid that this might be a practice that spreads to other Global South countries," Chen said.
"I think that is a major concern for not only for Taiwan, but also for other countries in the region and beyond."
Pakistan and China have maintained close diplomatic and strategic relations for decades, often describing their partnership as an "all-weather friendship" that is "higher than the Himalayas, deeper than the oceans, sweeter than honey and stronger than steel."
China is Pakistan's largest trading partner and a major investor, particularly through the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), and has poured tens of billions of dollars into funding massive transport, energy and infrastructure projects.

articles.title: Some 13 killed when Russian drone strikes trains in central Ukraine
articles.summary: At least 13 people were killed and 10 others wounded Thursday when a Russian jet-powered drone struck two trains stopped at a station in central Ukraine, officials said. Ukrainian...
articles.full_text:
At least 13 people were killed and 10 others wounded Thursday when a Russian jet-powered drone struck two trains stopped at a station in central Ukraine, officials said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described it in a post on X as a "horrific attack” that struck passenger trains in Dnipro.
"The Russians attacked the platform where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing. Unfortunately, as of now, 13 people have been confirmed dead," Zelenskyy said on social media.
"Fair and decisive actions by America and Europe are needed against Russian escalation," he added.
Dnipropetrovsk Regional Gov. Oleksandr Ganzha on Telegram said: "Thirteen people were killed in a Russian attack on Dnipro. At least five more were wounded."
Dnipro mayor Borys Filatov also lamented "a tragedy" in the city, saying on social media that "a drone hit a civilian electric train."
"Many people have been killed. Lots are wounded," he said.
The state Ukrainian Railways operator said a jet-powered Russian drone had hit the Dnipro train station.
"The strike hit one of the platforms, where train No. 866 Dnipro-Zaporizhzhia was at the time," it said on Telegram.
An elevated threat level had been announced, according to the rail company's chief, Oleksandr Pertsovsky.
"But unfortunately there were still a large number of people on the platform," he said on Facebook.
Russia has fired drones on trains across Ukraine since the first days of its 2022 invasion – destroying hundreds of locomotives and killing several railway workers.
In September alone, passengers were evacuated from more than 5,800 Ukrainian train services due to the threat of Russian drone strikes, the national railway operator told AFP.
The country's vast train network is a vital form of transport in the country, where journeys between east and west can take 24 hours.

articles.title: Rescuers scour Spain train wreck for survivors as country mourns
articles.summary: Rescuers searched wrecked rail cars Thursday for more survivors of Spain's second deadly high-speed train crash this year, which has killed 68 people. Emergency workers were seen c...
articles.full_text:
Rescuers searched wrecked rail cars Thursday for more survivors of Spain's second deadly high-speed train crash this year, which has killed 68 people.
Emergency workers were seen carrying what appeared to be a body wrapped in a blanket from one of the trains in a rural area in the central province of Toledo as cranes worked through the night to lift parts of the wreckage of Wednesday's crash.
"Rescue teams are still working very carefully, because we still cannot say with certainty that there are no more victims trapped in the twisted wreckage," Esther Padilla, a spokeswoman for the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha, told TVE.
"A canine unit was deployed yesterday. They will go back in today to make sure that nobody else remains there," she added.
Meanwhile, train drivers in Spain went ahead with a previously planned strike to press for more investment in railway safety after Europe's deadliest train accident since a 2013 derailment in Santiago de Compostela, Spain.
The crash, which followed another fatal accident in January involving the same rail companies on the same line, has also upended campaigning for a Nov. 29 snap election, with the leaders of Spain's two main parties suspending campaign events.
Spain's government has declared three days of national mourning for those killed when one high-speed train hit another.
Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez was due to travel to Toledo Thursday morning to take part in a meeting to monitor and coordinate the emergency response.
Meanwhile, Alberto Nunez Feijoo, leader of the center-right People's Party, which is currently leading in polls, was due to travel to the town of Urda near the crash site.
The crash has reopened a debate about safety on Spain's railways, Europe's longest and until recently a source of pride in the country.
Spanish Transport Minister Oscar Puente said Wednesday the crash happened after several trains stopped automatically due to a signal failure.
A state-run Renfe train was then authorized to proceed at normal speed even though there was a stationary Iryo-operated train ahead.
SEMAF, the Spanish train drivers' union, said it did not want to speculate on the cause of the crash.
"We wish to exercise caution until we have a detailed understanding of exactly what happened, so as not to engage in speculation," SEMAF said in a statement late Wednesday.
SEMAF said train drivers would proceed with the strike, planned before the accident to press for structural changes in railway safety, and that it was considering further action.

articles.title: Bolsonaro claims to be Brazil's rightful leader after escape to US
articles.summary: Brazil’s defeated right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro insisted Wednesday that he was the country’s rightful leader after fleeing to the United States in self-imposed...
articles.full_text:
Brazil’s defeated right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro insisted Wednesday that he was the country’s rightful leader after fleeing to the United States in self-imposed exile.
His defiance on arrival in Florida signaled continued upheaval for Brazil, where leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won a dramatic runoff election Sunday.
"I am the elected president and the criminals who stole Brazil's election are part of a criminal organization that has established a tyranny," Bolsonaro said in a statement published on his X account, denouncing "electoral fraud."
"I will lead the opposition from here," he said. In a subsequent statement, he revised his claim, saying he is the "leader," rather than "president."
Bolsonaro, 45, touched down earlier Wednesday on a private jet at Opa-Locka Executive Airport near Miami.
Rogerio Marinho, the leader of Bolsonaro's Liberal Party in the Senate, told reporters in Brasilia that he was in "solidarity" with the former candidate, describing him as a "political exile."
However, he distanced himself from Bolsonaro's statement and refused to back up Bolsonaro's claims of electoral fraud.
"The Liberal Party cannot make that claim," he said. "There is no evidence of that."
Flavio Bolsonaro "is an expression of the right in Brazil today ... he calls himself a leader and it's true: he's a leader," Marinho told reporters.
U.S. President Donald Trump's hard-right administration has strong links to Bolsonaro and his father, Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest in Brazil after attempting to overturn his own electoral loss to Lula in 2022.
Trump reiterated his view that Brazil's election was "very strange" but told reporters he "won't get involved" in Flavio Bolsonaro's claim to the presidency.
Details of how Bolsonaro, accompanied by his wife and daughters, reached the United States are still emerging.
He is under investigation in his home country over alleged corruption and money laundering. With his current parliamentary immunity about to expire, he was ordered to surrender his passports but left anyway, reaching the United States via Argentina and Ecuador.
A police source told Agence France-Presse (AFP) that Bolsonaro's Brazilian and diplomatic passports had been canceled, but the senator has also held Italian nationality since 2023, according to Italian documents seen by AFP.
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that the Bolsonaro family members were inspected and cleared "with applicable immigration laws and procedures."
The travel ban was issued by Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who led the case against Bolsonaro's father and is fiercely criticized by the Brazilian right.
Lula, who won Sunday's election with 51.8% of the vote, called Bolsonaro's departure a "shameful" act.
"A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide," he said in Brasilia during his 81st birthday celebration Tuesday.
But Brazilian police issued a statement Wednesday saying that he was not considered a fugitive.
There was controversy in neighboring Argentina, where opposition lawmakers demanded to know how Bolsonaro had managed to transit through the country.
While Argentinian authorities said he was carrying valid travel documents, officials have asked Cabinet chief Diego Santilli to provide details to Parliament, according to opposition lawmaker Agustin Rossi.
The most high-profile fraud case against Bolsonaro in Brazil centers on the unreleased biopic "Dark Horse," starring U.S. actor Jim Caviezel as Flavio's father, Jair.
In May, the outlet Intercept Brasil revealed audio recordings in which Flavio Bolsonaro negotiated approximately $24 million to finance the film with banker Daniel Vorcaro, who is jailed over one of Brazil's biggest fraud cases.
Before the leak, Flavio Bolsonaro had denied knowing Vorcaro or that the banker had financed the movie.
In July, the Supreme Court ordered a probe into the film's financing and whether it involved corruption, money laundering or the illegal movement of currency.
Bolsonaro acknowledged Vorcaro had funded the film but insisted it was a private business deal that was "completely legal."

articles.title: From reunification to Med deal: Türkiye-Libya relations take new turn
articles.summary: This month will likely be remembered as a key period in Turkish-Libyan relations. First, Libya’s House of Representatives approved a long-dormant memorandum of understanding on mar...
articles.full_text:
This month will likely be remembered as a key period in Turkish-Libyan relations. First, Libya’s House of Representatives approved a long-dormant memorandum of understanding on maritime jurisdiction and then came a critical meeting apparently kept under wraps for the reunification of Libya’s eastern and western administrations.
Overall, it appears that Türkiye’s diplomatic efforts are paying off, and doubly so: strengthening the country’s clout in the Mediterranean at a time its adversaries (including former ones such as Greece, with which Ankara hopes to mend ties) make their moves with new alliances and reinvigorating ties with North Africa, where post-Moammar Gadhafi Libya is still a key actor despite factions at odds.
On Oct. 20, Libya’s House of Representatives greenlit a maritime jurisdiction agreement with Türkiye, which has been awaiting approval since it was signed in 2019. Last Friday, media reports revealed that the eastern and western administrations in Libya sent delegates to Ankara for talks on a possible reunification. A senior Turkish official told Agence France-Presse (AFP) on Wednesday that talks have not produced an immediate result yet, but discussions focused on military reunification, with talks on political unity expected to follow in the future. Still, it is a beginning facilitated by Ankara, which rose to prominence in the last decade as a key power broker and mediator in its region and beyond.
Answering Daily Sabah’s questions about whether Libya’s House of Representatives’ decision cemented Türkiye’s influence in the region, Aylin Ünver Noi, professor of International Relations and vice rector of Beykoz University, said that the approval process made an important contribution.
“We are also seeing a process come to the fore that aligns with Türkiye’s interests in the region and reflects what Türkiye wants to achieve. However, there is something else worth keeping in mind. Türkiye has a policy regarding gas exploration and extraction activities in the Eastern Mediterranean and, more broadly, across the entire Mediterranean basin. It is trying to manage this process through bilateral relations, but at the same time, it has consistently maintained the same position from the very beginning. Türkiye says it is open to dialogue with all the countries that share maritime boundaries in the region,” she said.
Greece has long opposed the memorandum, fearing that Türkiye could gain greater influence in the Mediterranean. Athens views Türkiye as a historic rival, even as Ankara pursues rapprochement with Greece, and the deal could further complicate the maritime dispute between the two countries in the Aegean Sea.
Türkiye and Greece compete for rights in the vast sea. Soon after the deal was approved, Türkiye announced a navigational telex (Navtex) in the Mediterranean (a notice containing navigational and maritime safety warnings), citing work on a natural gas pipeline project between Türkiye and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) until late December. Like the France-led project, the gas pipeline will be a lifeline for the TRNC, which has been isolated from the international community, which refuses to recognize its sovereignty. The pipeline will connect Türkiye’s Mersin to the TRNC’s Girne (Kyrenia), covering a distance of about 101 kilometers (63 miles), including a 4-kilometer pipeline across land.
The Türkiye-Libya deal also drew the ire of the European Union, which counts Greece and the Greek Cypriot administration among its members.
If Ankara were able to implement the agreement, Türkiye could gain access to large, undiscovered gas deposits, but the deal covers a vast area claimed by Greece.
Noi said Türkiye sought to de-escalate tensions in the Med, with President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan even offering a meeting in Antalya to resolve the issue, referring to the Turkish leader’s proposal to find a formula safeguarding the interests of every littoral country.
“This position has not changed. Türkiye continues to pursue it. In his latest statement, the president also said that Türkiye is not trying to do anything against anyone. Rather, it is working toward arrangements that would allow everyone to benefit and produce a win-win outcome,” she said, referring to the president’s remarks after a Cabinet meeting earlier this week.
“But that does not mean Türkiye would accept a situation in which some countries gain disproportionately while others are deprived of their rights. In other words, Türkiye wants these partnerships, but it also wants the process to be managed in a way that prevents any country from pursuing maximalist claims at the expense of others. Türkiye wants everyone to be included and no party to be excluded,” she added.
She said Türkiye in the past was excluded from forums on the Eastern Mediterranean. “It was treated as though it had no coastline in the Eastern Mediterranean and no legitimate rights or interests in the region. Today, however, we see that these agreements have set a different process in motion, with Türkiye also beginning to normalize bilateral relations with certain countries. But this does not mean that the president is pursuing this process against anyone. Rather, the message is that Türkiye is not doing this to target others, but to ensure that no one is allowed to undermine its rights,” she also stated.
Erdoğan on Monday underlined that opposition to the Libya memorandum, particularly by the European Union, had no legitimate basis. In his address after the Cabinet meeting, the president stressed Türkiye’s policy on the Eastern Mediterranean was very clear, and they had no intention “to score a goal against anyone.”
“We are only occupied with preserving our maritime jurisdiction, rights and interests. We advocate for a peaceful approach to resolve disputes, engaging in dialogue with all littoral countries. We expect all actors, the European Union in particular, to demonstrate the same constructive will,” Erdoğan said.
He noted that the aggressive discourse benefited no one. “Even if it means paying a price, we never hesitate in doing the right thing for Türkiye, for the Turkish nation. I remind those trying to exclude Türkiye from the Eastern Mediterranean to respect the joint will of Türkiye and Libya,” he added.
Another interest for Türkiye in Libya is ensuring political stability, as Ankara stands to gain from finding a new partner in Africa where, under the leadership of Erdoğan, it has significantly enhanced relations through its “Africa opening” policy.
Since last year, dialogue between Ankara and rival groups in Libya has increased as the country reached out to Khalifa Haftar, with whom it once had tensions. Haftar’s son, Saddam Haftar, who holds a prominent military position, and Turkish officials have held frequent talks in recent months.
Noi said that since the Arab Spring, Türkiye has had to contend with a situation shaped by the consequences of those uprisings. “They gave rise to problems such as civil wars and failed states in many parts of the region. This triggered a process that undermined the stability of those countries and negatively affected their relations with other nations. Countries that are divided and governed by different groups or rival leaderships also face another disadvantage: external powers can support different factions, further destabilizing these countries and undermining peace and development. From the very beginning of the Arab Spring, Türkiye has opposed the fragmentation of countries and the emergence of failed states, whether in Syria or Libya. On the contrary, it has consistently emphasized principles such as territorial integrity and independence,” she said.
“The same applies to Libya. Bringing the two opposing sides together would strengthen Libya as a unified country. This is something Türkiye wants, both in terms of regional stability and the development of its bilateral relations. However, Türkiye's role must not be destabilizing; on the contrary, its support has always been aimed at promoting stability,” she added.
Noi noted that Türkiye played a significant role in mediation efforts in recent years, and these efforts were institutionalized within the Foreign Ministry, which established a directorate-general for mediation.
“Türkiye has made considerable progress in this field, with successful initiatives in various parts of the world, including mediation efforts across the African continent. Therefore, Türkiye may have taken an important step in Libya by helping bring together groups that have been at odds within the country. Türkiye has already pursued a similar approach in Syria, as you know. It supports a unified Syria and wants groups pursuing separatist aims to be reintegrated into the country. Türkiye has never sought the division, fragmentation or weakening of its neighbors or other countries in the region. Instead, it has wanted them to remain unified, strong and capable of contributing to regional stability. This would be an important development both for bilateral relations and for the future and survival of the country concerned. That is what Türkiye hopes to achieve. We have already seen progress in this direction in recent days,” she said.

articles.title: Human error or system failure? Spain probes deadly train crash
articles.summary: Spain’s second major train collision this year has reignited questions over whether human error or systemic failures in its once-praised high-speed rail network are to blame. The c...
articles.full_text:
Spain’s second major train collision this year has reignited questions over whether human error or systemic failures in its once-praised high-speed rail network are to blame.
The causes remain disputed.
Spain’s transport minister has pointed to a traffic controller’s alleged poor judgment as a key factor in Wednesday’s crash in Toledo province, which claimed 69 lives.
Railway unions, however, reject the focus on individual responsibility, arguing that worsening working conditions have left the network increasingly vulnerable. They cite a shortage of traffic controllers, heavier workloads and mounting pressure on staff responsible for the safety of some 45 million passengers each year.
A judge and a special government commission are conducting separate investigations into the deadly collision, while Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has pledged a thorough inquiry to establish what caused the disaster.
"This investigation must determine how and why this catastrophe happened," Spain’s King Felipe VI said Thursday after visiting injured passengers at a hospital in Toledo. "We will have to take measures so this never happens again."
The chain of events that led to the disaster began at 8:30 a.m. Wednesday, when the communication system essential to the line’s safety operations went down. Known as LZB, the system monitors train positions and can automatically activate a train’s brakes to prevent collisions.
The malfunction forced human controllers at a control center in Madrid to assume full responsibility for monitoring train movements and safety along a 63-kilometer (39-mile) stretch between Madrid and Seville. Authorities believe six trains were on the affected section at the time.
At 8:36 a.m., a controller told a train operated by state-owned RENFE that it could resume normal-speed operations. Another train, operated by privately owned IRYO and located 15.5 miles (25 kilometers) farther down the line, also attempted to restart, but its engineer was unable to override the automatic stop and notified the controller.
At 8:53 a.m., the trains collided, derailing carriages and leaving parts of the wreckage torn apart.
It was the second major crash on the Madrid-Seville line this year. In January, farther south along the route, a train derailed and struck another traveling in the opposite direction, killing 46 people.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente, who is facing calls to resign, described the controller’s decision to allow one train to resume at full speed while the other remained stopped as "inexplicable" and "erroneous."
Puente said the RENFE train should never have been authorized to move because a stop signal was still active on the line.
"An order is given for the train to restart, an erroneous decision," Puente told reporters. The decision "was taken in inexplicable circumstances given that a train was stopped and with a red light," he said.
Railway unions, however, argue that the circumstances surrounding the decision cannot be ignored.
Raquel Ayllon, a spokesperson for SCF, Spain’s railway traffic controllers union, told The Associated Press that workloads regularly exceed what existing staff can safely manage. She said controllers have been calling for additional personnel for years while safety systems continue to fail.
"We believe (the minister) is blaming a mere worker who was working under increasingly poor conditions," she said. "Human error isn't incomprehensible. What is incomprehensible is that the safety system is regularly failing."
SEMAF, Spain’s train engineers union, said the three-decade-old LZB safety system, which remains in use on the Madrid-Seville line as it is gradually phased out, has failed before, leaving human operators to manage train movements without its protection.
"The LZB system should have been replaced some time ago," said Diego Martin, a SEMAF spokesperson. "It failed us yesterday (Wednesday) and it has gone offline on repeated occasions in the past."
Railway workers went on strike Thursday in a previously planned action to demand that the government honor its commitments to improve safety conditions following the January crash.
Representatives of several unions also condemned what they described as the "irresponsible" leak of audio recordings of conversations between the control center and train engineers to Spanish media outlets.
Spain’s railways were exclusively operated by state-owned companies until the country opened its high-speed passenger network to private operators in 2021.
Both major crashes this year involved trains operated by RENFE and IRYO.
Rail traffic has increased since the market was opened to competition. Between Madrid and Barcelona, for example, the average number of daily services rose from 56 in 2019 to 89 in 2024, according to the SCF union.
Joan Rodriguez, a spokesperson for a Spanish railway workers union, said the increase in traffic following privatization had placed additional pressure on the network.
"We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines," Rodriguez told Spanish public broadcaster TVE on Wednesday. "I am not saying it was a determining factor (in the crashes), but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind."
