articles.title: Bolsonaro's self-exile, ChatGPT blunder cloud political ambitions
articles.summary: Brazilian Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro has faced widespread ridicule and mounting political isolation after fleeing to the United States and declaring himself Brazil's rightful leader fol...
articles.full_text:
Brazilian Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro has faced widespread ridicule and mounting political isolation after fleeing to the United States and declaring himself Brazil's rightful leader following his defeat in Sunday's presidential election.
The 45-year-old's claims sparked a wave of mockery on Brazilian social media, where pop star Anitta jokingly declared herself free of cellulite, one influencer proclaimed himself the "true president" of Twitter, and another announced he had won the next lottery.
The eldest son of former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro stunned Brazil's political establishment Wednesday when he published a statement challenging the election outcome and presenting himself as the country's legitimate leader. The declaration, however, quickly became an embarrassment after a series of confusing revisions and failed to win support from influential figures within his own political camp.
Flavio Bolsonaro arrived in Miami on Wednesday after leaving Brazil through Argentina and Ecuador, despite a Supreme Court order requiring him to surrender his passports as part of ongoing investigations, including a money laundering probe in which he denies wrongdoing.
Hours after arriving in the United States, he published a statement on social media proclaiming himself Brazil's "true president-elect." About an hour later, he deleted the document and replaced it with a revised version describing himself as the country's "leader."
The abrupt change prompted questions about the original statement, which also featured an outdated version of Brazil's coat of arms, abandoned in the 1960s.
A close Bolsonaro ally, right-wing influencer and podcast host Paulo Figueiredo, later blamed the errors on ChatGPT, saying the chatbot had been used to help prepare the document.
Figueiredo, who acts as an unofficial spokesperson for the Bolsonaro family in the United States and initially circulated the statement to journalists, said the document had passed through several drafts involving multiple contributors.
According to Figueiredo, Flavio's younger brother, former Congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, sought ChatGPT's assistance in finalizing the letter. The chatbot allegedly inserted an earlier version of the text and an outdated national emblem.
"When generating the document, AI ended up including an earlier version of the text, in which Flavio presented himself as the true 'president-elect'," Figueiredo wrote on X, adding that the mistakes were discovered only after the document had been distributed to the press.
He said Flavio eventually chose the word "leader" for legal and moral reasons, describing the changes as minor and claiming those involved found the mistake amusing.
OpenAI and Flavio Bolsonaro's press officers did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Despite the revised wording, Figueiredo maintained that the senator considered Sunday's election illegitimate and intended to continue challenging the result.
The declaration drew widespread condemnation in Brazilian media, with several outlets describing its language as an attempt to undermine democratic institutions.
O Globo newspaper likened Flavio Bolsonaro to a "lunatic asylum Napoleon," while Folha de S.Paulo dismissed the statement as "pathetic."
Politicians across the political spectrum called for the election results to be respected, further exposing the senator's isolation.
Among the most significant rebukes came from Sao Paulo Gov. Tarcisio de Freitas, a former minister under Jair Bolsonaro who had been considered a leading contender to represent the right in the next presidential race before the former president backed his son.
"We are democrats. The election result is sovereign. What we have seen is the will of the majority of the population, which must be respected," De Freitas told Estadao newspaper.
With Flavio now outside Brazil and his political standing weakened, attention has quickly shifted to who might emerge as the conservative movement's leading figure.
De Freitas, who enjoys strong support in business circles, acknowledged that a presidential bid in 2030 was a possibility.
Other prominent Bolsonaro allies have also rejected claims that the election was stolen.
Rogerio Marinho, who coordinated Flavio Bolsonaro's campaign, said there was no evidence of electoral fraud. Supreme Court Justice Kassio Nunes Marques, appointed by Jair Bolsonaro, also issued a statement defending the security and integrity of Brazil's electoral process.
The election authority and international observers have recognized the result, while leaders around the world have acknowledged Lula's victory.
Despite his defeat, Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to lead the opposition from the United States, seeking to maintain his influence over Brazil's conservative movement while remaining outside the country.
His departure has not, however, translated into an immediate loss of political strength for the right. Conservatives secured substantial representation in Congress, and Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL) is expected to hold the largest number of seats when the new legislature begins its term in February.
But political analyst Geraldo Monteiro of the State University of Rio de Janeiro said Flavio's attempt to establish himself as a leader in exile was unlikely to command the loyalty he expected.
Rather than a political misstep, Monteiro described the declaration as a calculated effort to preserve his authority over the conservative camp.
"I do not believe he has the means to lead the opposition from afar, as the newly elected officials have already secured their seats and no longer need him," Monteiro told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
He said the statement had drawn a dividing line within the right between politicians willing to demonstrate unwavering loyalty to the Bolsonaro family and those unwilling to become involved in another attempt to undermine democratic institutions.
Monteiro also drew parallels between Flavio's conduct and that of his father, who was sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 presidential election to Lula.
The backlash has extended to the leadership of Bolsonaro's own party.
On Thursday, PL leader Valdemar Costa Neto visited Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving his sentence under house arrest. Asked about Flavio's statement afterward, Costa Neto made clear that the party was not endorsing the declaration.
"No one approves" of the letter, he said, adding that the party needed to "move forward."

articles.title: Africa battles Ebola surge as ministers reject border closures
articles.summary: African health ministers have agreed to keep their countries' borders open while strengthening surveillance and cross-border cooperation as an Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Repu...
articles.full_text:
African health ministers have agreed to keep their countries' borders open while strengthening surveillance and cross-border cooperation as an Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues to spread, with more than 10,000 confirmed cases and nearly 5,000 deaths.
The decision followed an emergency virtual meeting convened by the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), attended by more than 40 health ministers who discussed ways to contain the outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus.
The meeting agreed that countries should prepare their health systems for potential infections, coordinate their responses and closely monitor cross-border movements rather than impose widespread border closures.
Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya warned that the continent was falling behind in its efforts to contain the outbreak, which has a case fatality rate of 48.5%, according to the agency.
"I stood before more than 40 African ministers and said what the data tells us: We are not winning so far," Kaseya said.
"Together, we agreed to prepare every country, coordinate across our borders and keep those borders open while watching them closely. Our partners are standing behind Africa's plan."
Kaseya said the outbreak had evolved over five months from a national emergency into a continental health security challenge, with insecurity, humanitarian crises and limited funding complicating containment efforts.
Uganda's Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi said his country's experience showed that early detection and decisive action could interrupt transmission.
Uganda was declared free of Ebola by the World Health Organization (WHO) in August after reporting 20 confirmed cases following the outbreak's declaration in May.
The Africa CDC has identified 10 other countries at risk, including Rwanda, Kenya, Tanzania, Angola, Burundi, the Central African Republic, the Republic of Congo, Ethiopia, South Sudan and Zambia.
The outbreak has surpassed 10,170 confirmed cases, making it the second-largest Ebola epidemic on record. Some experts fear it could eventually overtake the 2014-2016 West African outbreak, which infected about 28,000 people and killed more than 11,000.
Although researchers disagree over whether the current epidemic will reach that scale, they warn that the risk of further international spread will increase unless transmission in the DRC is brought under control.
The country is reporting between 400 and 500 new confirmed infections each week, with numbers remaining relatively stable.
Dr. Boghuma Titanji, an infectious disease specialist at Emory University, said the figures offered limited encouragement because infections were neither rising exponentially nor declining.
One major obstacle is the difficulty of tracing contacts and securing cooperation from affected communities. Health workers have sometimes spent more time persuading residents to cooperate than providing medical assistance.
Fewer than a quarter of new cases involve people already identified as contacts of infected individuals, suggesting that numerous transmission chains remain undetected.
France, Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda have also reported cases linked to the outbreak, with approximately 30 confirmed infections recorded outside the DRC.
Justin Lessler, a University of North Carolina researcher who studies infectious disease outbreaks, said the direct threat to the United States remained extremely low but warned that countries with fragile health systems could face greater difficulties.
South Sudan, particularly vulnerable because of conflict and humanitarian challenges, is among the countries of concern.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people, including blood, vomit and semen. Controlling transmission therefore requires effective isolation, contact tracing and infection prevention measures.
The current outbreak has been particularly difficult to contain because it is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a strain related to but distinct from the Ebola virus responsible for most previous epidemics.
Initial diagnostic testing was primarily designed to detect the more familiar Ebola virus, delaying recognition of the strain behind the current infections. Although the outbreak was declared in May, medical evidence suggests transmission had begun months earlier.
Armed conflict, weaknesses in health systems, community mistrust, misinformation and reductions in international aid have further complicated the response.
Katie Thomas-Canfield, the International Rescue Committee's Ebola response director, said working directly with affected communities was essential to breaking transmission chains.
Dr. Wendy Armstrong, president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America, warned that the outbreak remained far from being controlled and could deteriorate further.
Experts expect transmission to continue through the end of the year, although vaccine development offers hope for 2027. Several candidates are being tested against the Bundibugyo strain, and Titanji said she was optimistic an effective vaccine could become available within the next 12 months.
Meanwhile, researchers are updating projections to assess how the epidemic could develop.
In May, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) published computer-generated scenarios estimating that infections could reach between 10,000 and more than 20,000 over three months. The agency is updating its projections but declined to make scientists available to The Associated Press (AP) to discuss the latest trends.
Alessandro Vespignani, a disease modeler at Northeastern University, said weekly infections had yet to decline enough to signal meaningful progress.
He said there had not been the kind of "decay in the number of cases weekly that we need to see the light at the end of the tunnel."

articles.title: Russian barrage kills 20 across Ukraine despite hopes for truce
articles.summary: A Russian drone strike killed at least 14 people at a crowded railway station in Dnipro on Thursday, while separate daytime attacks killed five more people in two other Ukrainian c...
articles.full_text:
A Russian drone strike killed at least 14 people at a crowded railway station in Dnipro on Thursday, while separate daytime attacks killed five more people in two other Ukrainian cities.
A late-night missile strike on the capital, Kyiv, killed another person, officials said.
The wave of attacks rocked Ukrainian cities as a local cease-fire in the southern Kherson region raised cautious hopes for a possible resumption of diplomatic efforts.
"Russia is deliberately hunting civilians: on trains, at stations, in residential buildings," Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretskyi said in a statement on Telegram.
"There is no justification for this terror, and there never can be."
Another Russian missile attack struck several districts of Kyiv shortly before 11:00 p.m. (9:00 p.m. GMT), killing one person, the city's military administration said. The attack set warehouses ablaze, while falling debris damaged a building on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River.
A few hours earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had described the attacks as "very cruel" and "deliberate when everyone expects de-escalation steps."
Zelenskyy warned that Ukraine had intelligence "about preparations by the Russians of new ballistic missile strikes. We need the means to take out all this Russian evil. We are expecting relevant decisions."
The six-day truce, brokered with U.S. help, applied only to the southern Kherson region, where a humanitarian mission was underway to deliver aid to the Russian-held town of Oleshky, which has been isolated in a war zone since the start of Moscow's 2022 invasion.
Both sides issued virtually identical statements saying demining operations had been completed and the mission could proceed, allowing aid to reach the town and giving residents the opportunity to leave if they wished.
Elsewhere, Russian drone and missile attacks on critical infrastructure, including the rail network, have disrupted civilian life and ravaged the economy. The strikes have been compounded by an acute shortage of air defense missiles.
Bodies scattered across platform
In Dnipro, state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia said a jet-powered drone had struck a platform at the city's main railway station, where a commuter train was preparing to depart.
Mangled bodies lay scattered across the pavement, which was marked by shrapnel, as pools of bright red blood collected nearby. Police placed bodies in black bags amid the wail of an air-raid siren.
"And for what? What goal are they (Russians) trying to achieve?" said Svitlana Shcherbak, 67, as she sheltered underground at the station. "I don't understand it at all."
Another attack on Dnipro struck a student dormitory, setting it ablaze, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. He added that a day of attacks had cut power to 350,000 households in the city.
Russia's escalating bombing campaign against Ukrainian cities has repeatedly killed civilians. Moscow has denied targeting civilians.
Two teenage girls were killed on a central street in Chernihiv in northern Ukraine, while three people died in strikes on residential buildings in the central city of Kremenchuk.
In Chernihiv, 23 people, including four children, were wounded in a drone attack on a busy downtown street, in addition to the two teenagers killed.
"Ordinary, peaceful people were attacked who were just going to work, going about their daily business, making plans for the day," said Dmytro Bryzhynskyi, head of the city's military administration.
In Kremenchuk, strikes on a residential block and private buildings killed three people and wounded 32, the regional governor said. Russian drones also struck city buses in three separate attacks in Zaporizhzhia in southeastern Ukraine, wounding six people, officials said.
Thursday's strikes came amid renewed efforts to revive U.S.-backed peace talks to end Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II.
New three-way talks are expected to take place next month, with Ukrainian officials, including top presidential adviser Kyrylo Budanov, urging Kyiv's partners to increase pressure on Moscow.

articles.title: 'Mushroom killer' Patterson's appeal fails as court locks in life sentence
articles.summary: An Australian appeals court on Friday ruled that triple murderer Erin Patterson must spend the rest of her life in prison, citing the “shocking criminality” of her poisoning four r...
articles.full_text:
An Australian appeals court on Friday ruled that triple murderer Erin Patterson must spend the rest of her life in prison, citing the “shocking criminality” of her poisoning four relatives of her estranged husband with deadly death cap mushrooms.
A three-judge panel of Victoria state’s Court of Appeal dismissed Patterson’s challenge to her convictions and upheld prosecutors’ appeal against the leniency of her original sentence. The ruling set aside her 33-year non-parole period, which would have made her eligible for parole consideration at age 82.
“The offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated and stands to be denounced in the strongest terms,” Justice Stephen McLeish said on behalf of the three judges.
“After anxious consideration, we have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a nonparole period,” McLeish added.
Patterson is among the very few women in Australian history to receive a life sentence without the possibility of parole.
The first woman to receive such a sentence was Katherine Knight, a meatworker sentenced in New South Wales in 2001 for murdering her partner, John Price, the previous year. Knight stabbed Price at least 37 times.
Patterson’s convictions stemmed from a family lunch she hosted at her rural home in Leongatha in July 2023, where she served four relatives beef Wellington dishes laced with poisonous death cap mushrooms.
She was found guilty of murdering her former parents-in-law, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail’s sister, Heather Wilkinson. Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, survived after spending weeks in the hospital but was also the victim of an attempted murder for which Patterson was convicted.
Patterson was sentenced in September 2025 to three life terms for murder and 25 years in prison for the attempted murder of Ian Wilkinson. The sentences included a 33-year nonparole period.
She may still seek special leave to appeal to Australia’s High Court, the country’s highest judicial authority, although doing so would require meeting a high legal threshold.
Patterson has maintained her innocence and denied deliberately poisoning her relatives.
The deaths of Don and Gail Patterson and Heather Wilkinson within days of the lunch attracted widespread international media attention, turning the case into one of Australia’s most closely followed criminal trials.
The case has also inspired podcasts, books and screen adaptations.
Emmy-nominated actor Melanie Lynskey announced this week that she will portray Erin Patterson in a six-episode series for Paramount+, a subscription video-on-demand streaming service.
Lynskey will also serve as an executive producer on the series, which will dramatize the 97 days between the fatal lunch and Patterson’s arrest.
Prosecutors argued during an appeal hearing in August that Patterson should never become eligible for parole, saying her original sentence failed to reflect the calculated nature of the crimes.
McLeish said Patterson’s intention to murder all four lunch guests had been sustained for nearly three weeks, from the time she invited them to the meal through the preparation and serving of the poisoned food.
The judge also pointed to what he described as an “elaborate series of deceptions,” including Patterson’s false claims about having cancer, which she used to explain why her two children would not attend the lunch.
The only survivor, Ian Wilkinson, testified that Patterson had told her guests she wanted their advice on what to tell the children about her supposed diagnosis.
McLeish also noted that Patterson had destroyed evidence, denied foraging for mushrooms and repeatedly made false claims about where the mushrooms had come from.
“The offending was carefully planned and deliberate. It represented a cruel breach of trust,” McLeish said.
Patterson chose not to attend Friday’s hearing in person and watched the proceedings via video link from prison.
Because of her notoriety, she is held in the high-security Gordon Unit of Melbourne’s Dame Phyllis Frost Centre, a women’s prison where inmates considered at high risk from other prisoners are housed for their protection.
During her sentencing in September 2025, trial judge Christopher Beale said there was a “substantial chance” Patterson could remain in solitary confinement for years.
Patterson’s estranged husband, Simon Patterson, had also been invited to the lunch but declined the invitation the day before.
Evidence presented before the trial revealed that Simon Patterson had previously expressed suspicions that his estranged wife might have tried to kill him.
He testified during a pretrial hearing that he declined the lunch invitation because he feared for his safety.
